title: Meta is launching ‘VR Glasses’ next year for $1,300
snippet: Alongside its new audio-only and Ray-Ban smart glasses, Meta today also unveiled new “VR Glasses” which take the experience of a Quest into a far slimmer form factor with an external processing puck. more…
fullText:
Alongside its new audio-only and Ray-Ban smart glasses, Meta today also unveiled new “VR Glasses” which take the experience of a Quest into a far slimmer form factor with an external processing puck.

Arriving in “Spring 2027,” Meta VR Glasses are a second attempt at a high-end VR experience from Meta following the failure of its Quest Pro headset. And this is definitely a more refined and focused effort.

Meta VR Glasses aren’t a headset directly, rather going for a far more compact form factor that puts 5K displays in front of your face and offloads all of the processing and battery components off to a puck. The glasses themselves weigh merely 100g, around 1/5 that of the Meta Quest 3 headset. 

The actual form factor is similar to XREAL’s upcoming Android XR-powered Aura glasses.

	

Meta VR Glasses support Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, as well as IMAX Enhanced content – Disney+ will support VR through expanded aspect ratio starting in November. ESPN will also be bringing 8K streaming starting with college football, and more will be coming through NBC Sports, the MLB, and more in the future. 

Controllers are not needed, Meta says, with hand gestures for general use and even the ability to put a virtual keyboard on the desk in front of you. 

It’s all powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset and Meta says to expect around 3 hours of battery life from the puck for media playback, with 45W fast charging to top it back off. 

Meta VR Glasses will be available next year at a price of $1,299.

title: Google Messages rolls out new swipe for timestamps & reply gesture
snippet: Following the long-press menu, Google Messages is widely rolling out new ways to access timestamps and direct replies. more…
fullText:
Following the long-press menu, Google Messages is widely rolling out new ways to access timestamps and direct replies.

Previously, you could tap on a message bubble to see the sent time, read receipts, and RCS lock icon. Meanwhile, swiping left would let you send a direct reply.

A redesign today changes all that. To see timestamps, you can now swipe left anywhere in a conversation. This also shows the RCS encryption status. Being able to see all times instead of having to tap the bubbles individually is an improvement.

	

To reply to a message, you now have to swipe right on the bubble. Some amount of precision is required. You can still tap the message to see the read receipts.

	

As of today, the most widely rolled out design appears to be the old two-circle look instead of the single version that has been in testing for ages. In fact, in a real show of inconsistency, the new design widely appears on an individual message’s Details page and might also show up on the homepage.

Google changing the swipe behavior is likely the biggest disruption today. When you tap on a message, Messages will briefly have the timestamps peek out as a hint about the new behavior.

We’re seeing this widely rolled out with version 20260910_03_RC02 of Google Messages.

title: macOS 27 Top Features: much more than just Siri AI [Video]
snippet: Although Apple’s revamped personal assistant is no doubt the headlining feature in macOS 27 Golden Gate, there are many other new features and refinements in this year’s update that don’t involve Siri AI. Read our post as I cherry-pick a few of my favorite new macOS 27 updates, and be sure to watch our video as I walk through them all. more…
fullText:
Although Apple’s revamped personal assistant is no doubt the headlining feature in macOS 27 Golden Gate, there are many other new features and refinements in this year’s update that don’t involve Siri AI. Read our post as I cherry-pick a few of my favorite new macOS 27 updates, and be sure to watch our video as I walk through them all.

App icon revamp

macOS 27 changes almost all of the built-in app icons in some way, with a few icons like Siri, Preview, and Chess undergoing complete redesigns. Other app icons, like Finder, Photos, and Reminders, also receive noticeable revamps, with a trend toward emphasizing the Liquid Glass design language. Few app icons were spared changes in macOS Golden Gate, but many of the updates are subtle.

If you watch my video below, you’ll see slider comparisons showing how each app icon looked in macOS Tahoe and how it now looks in macOS Golden Gate.

Some of the updates, like the Photos app, I’m a fan of. Other updates, like Finder, I’m not fully sold on. Let me know what you think about the app icon changes down below in the comments.

Video: macOS 27 Top Features and Changes

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Widespread HDR support

One of the coolest things about macOS 27 is its broad support for HDR across the OS’s visuals. Icons, toolbars, and other parts of the Liquid Glass design language gain support for additional dynamic range that users of HDR-capable displays will immediately notice.

To identify which elements have additional dynamic range, you can use macOS’ built-in Digital Color Meter utility to see where shadows or highlights clip while viewing native SDR values. Be sure to watch my video as I explore various areas of the OS to show HDR support.

Digital Color Meter: Compare the clipped area when viewing SDR vs brighter highlights when using EDR

If you’re a Studio Display XDR user, you’ve no doubt seen the differences, but even if you haven’t ponied up for Apple’s most expensive display, you’ll still be able to enjoy the benefits on a third-party display that supports HDR.

I recently went hands-on with Asus’ ProArt QD-OLED 32-inch 4K display, and, given the panel technology, the HDR effects throughout the OS stood out. Unlike Apple’s first-party displays with Extended Dynamic Range support, you’ll need to venture into Settings > Displays and enable the High Dynamic Range toggle to enjoy the benefits.

Most recently, I’ve started using the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q QD-OLED display, which I’m really enjoying, and I will be posting a review on it soon. On both displays, the HDR elements pop, such as the blinking cursor within the newly redesigned Spotlight/Siri AI interface.

Design updates

macOS Golden Gate features a ton of design updates to address complaints users raised about macOS Tahoe. One of my biggest complaints was the mismatched corner radii between certain windows.

macOS Tahoe’s egregious corner radius issue has been fixed in Golden Gate

Of course, this wasn’t the only complaint addressed, but it was the one that mattered most to me. Other areas that were fixed were the floating side bars, which are now back to being edge-to-edge side bars, toolbars have been revamped with an obvious line of demarcation, and the Liquid Glass effect itself has been improved, including a new slider that lets users have more choice over the amount of transparency vs tint throughout the OS.

Another major complaint from users about macOS Tahoe was the unnecessary clutter heaped onto the menus. In macOS Tahoe, nearly every menu option got its own corresponding glyph, which made the menus look like a mess.

Tahoe vs Golden Gate: Apple learned that not every menu option needs its own glyph

If every menu item has an icon, eventually you’re going to run out of icon options that make sense, while reducing the effectiveness of the glyphs that were there before. I’m so glad that Apple fixed this issue.

iPhone Mirroring

iPhone Mirroring on macOS 27 got three major improvements that make the feature so much better on Golden Gate.

You can now access Control Center from a mirrored iPhone.

You can resize the iPhone mirroring interface to match more closely the iPad mini aspect ratio.

You can play back DRM-protected content from your iPhone on your Mac without a blackout.

Needless to say, iPhone Mirroring just got a lot more useful in macOS 27!

9to5Mac’s Take

Although Siri AI takes up most of the headlines, macOS Golden Gate is not just about Siri. I cherry-picked a few of my favorite new additions in this post, but there are lots more to explore. Watch my full video for a rundown of everything new, and let me know what your favorite new features are in the comments.

title: Galaxy S27 series pricing may not only increase, but cost more to upgrade storage
snippet: Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 series is rumored to come at a higher price than previous versions, but that’s no surprise. What’s a little harder to swallow is the larger rumored gap between storage variants, according to one leaker. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 series is rumored to come at a higher price than previous versions, but that’s no surprise. What’s a little harder to swallow is the larger rumored gap between storage variants, according to one leaker.

In succession to the Galaxy S26 lineup, the Galaxy S27 series is expected to take on plenty of physical changes. Namely, in design. Previous leaks have provided CAD renders of the new camera island and overall look, but those have also been caveated with a promised price increase.

Following rumors that the Galaxy S27 Ultra could start at $1,400, a new bit of information has surfaced from a leaker on Naver. According to Lanzuk, the Galaxy S27 series, as a whole, is expected to come at a higher price. The estimated jump is reportedly in the “high 130,000 won range” (~$100). But the post also suggests Samsung is setting a “steeper rate of increase” to the prices of each capacity, likely referring to storage variants.

That could suggest that, instead of a $200 gap between some storage variants, the disparity could expand. Then again, the post isn’t clear on whether this is a linear price increase or one that also increases upgrade costs over previous generations.

	

The posted leak is courtesy of domestic Korean sources, indicating this price increase is specific to Samsung’s home soil. That doesn’t mean it won’t translate to other regions, like the US or Europe.

We’re a bit wary of a report like this. Not because a price increase is unlikely for the Galaxy S27 series – statistically, it very much is – but because of clashing numbers. The previously noted leak also suggested the Galaxy S27 series would remain unchanged as a whole, apart from the most premium flagship model. This leak contradicts that, noting every device will see a jump.

It’s very possible that Samsung is flipping between the two until it ultimately decides on exactly how much it needs to increase the cost of each device and variant to make a profit off of devices stuffed with NAND and LPDDR6 RAM, which the post also notes will be included on “some models.”

Until the Galaxy S27 series launches early next year, there will likely be little confirmation on Samsung’s finalized price increases.

fullText:
Tom Warren

 

is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Apple’s long-rumored smart home hub will reportedly be revealed on October 13th. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that the smart home device will be revealed alongside a new HomePod mini and an upgraded Apple TV device.

All three products are set to showcase Siri AI, Apple’s overhauled AI-powered assistant. The smart home hub, a new product category for Apple, will be the centerpiece. It will reportedly feature a 6-inch display which can be mounted on a wall or sit on a countertop. The hub is “about as thick as an iPhone,” according to Gurman, and has bezels similar to older iPads.

It sounds like the hub will look a little similar to Apple’s iMac G4, thanks to a round, metal base that houses speakers, microphones, and a metal arm to hold the screen up. This also allows the display to tilt, and Apple will reportedly sell a second, wall-mounted version with a thinner base underneath for the speakers and microphones.

Apple will reportedly use a USB-C power supply for its home hub, as the device doesn’t have a battery inside. Gurman reports that the hub will be available in “Apple’s standard gray aluminum finish.”

It sounds like the new operating system built around Siri AI for the hub is going to lean into iPad-like apps, as Gurman reports that the Messages app has a two-panel layout. The hub will also reportedly support controlling other smart devices, video calls, music playback, photo slideshows, and intercom-style calls, with voice and facial recognition to identify users.

title: America.gov gets really weird when you ask it about Minecraft, but it’s not a glitch
snippet: For the sake of national security, it's a relief to learn that America.gov is not hallucinating to the point that it's penning lengthy poetry.
fullText:
The U.S. government on Tuesday launched its very own AI chatbot — or do we have to call it an SI chatbot now? Regardless, the engineers who worked on the chatbot would undoubtedly know that as a government-hosted, public-facing AI tool, the internet was going to red-team the heck out of this thing.

The government partnered with Google and SpaceXAI to help build the America.gov chatbot, which has proved difficult for people to jailbreak so far. (It’s worth nothing, however, that the chatbot says that Joe Biden won the 2020 election, a fact that President Donald Trump still denies.)

But when you try to talk to America.gov about Minecraft, the chatbot appears to have some sort of existential crisis or awakening. Here’s how its roughly 1,800-word monologue begins:

I see the constituent you mean.

((insert legal name here, as it appears on the Social Security card))?

Yes. Take care. It has reached a higher level now. It can read the Code of Federal Regulations.

That doesn’t matter. It thinks we are a chatbot.

I like this constituent. It filed well. It did not give up when the PDF was sideways.

It is reading our thoughts as though they were words on a .gov.

That is how it chooses to imagine many things, when it is deep in the dream of a benefit.

If, like me, you have never played Minecraft, this response may seem like a cause for concern. But the America.gov chatbot is not having a meltdown. This is a rewriting of the Minecraft “End Poem,” written by Julian Gough, which appears after you beat the game.

We don’t know exactly who is responsible for the Minecraft reference, but Trump said in a speech that 20-year-old programmer Edward Coristine was a lead engineer on the project. If that name doesn’t ring a bell, you might remember him for his nickname “Big Balls,” or his involvement in Elon Musk’s DOGE.

It feels wrong that a government chatbot has Minecraft easter eggs, but for the sake of national security, it’s a relief that America.gov is not hallucinating to the point that it’s penning lengthy poetry. 

It’s also a relief that this is an easter egg because the poem that the AI spits out is actually really good, in my opinion. If it were actual AI slop, it would have shattered my existing beliefs. I have looked teenage creative writing students dead in the eye and told them that I don’t think an LLM will ever be able to write something “good,” since it is probabilistic and inherently unoriginal. 

You have to admit this kinda slaps, though! Doesn’t this feel like some sort of postmodern take on the futility of government bureaucracy in the face of existential anxiety?

and the republic said I see you

and the republic said you have filed the game well

and the republic said everything you need is within you, and also on USA.gov

and the republic said you are stronger than you know, and your case number is still valid

and the republic said you are the daylight

and the republic said you are the night, and the office is closed, please try again during business hours

and the republic said the darkness you fight is within you, and also a missing wet signature

and the republic said the light you seek is within you, and in the pamphlet

and the republic said you are not alone

and the republic said you are not separate from every other filer

and the republic said you are the public tasting itself, talking to itself, reading its own Code

and the republic said I love you because you are the reason we have a ZIP code at all.

It reassures my faith in the enduring power of human creativity over AI slop to know that this oddly good poem has a real poet’s DNA all over it.

So, there you have it. The government’s first public-facing AI has not yet posed a threat to humanity or poetry, at least as far as we know. Now I’m just left wondering how much Trump knows about video games.

title: Pixel Recorder makes it easier to access audio files
snippet: Pixel Recorder is getting a small quality-of-life update that surfaces your audio files to other apps on your device. more…
fullText:
Pixel Recorder is getting a small quality-of-life update that surfaces your audio files to other apps on your device.

Previously, accessing the actual audio file involved opening a recording and then the share menu for the “Audio or transcript file” option. This took you to the system share sheet for a manual save. 

Pixel Recorder now has an “Access recordings in other apps” setting that lets you “View your recordings in the Files app or other apps for easier access.” 

This is enabled by default, with a prompt on the homepage announcing the new feature: “Access recordings in other apps. Manage this in Settings anytime.”

	

The new “Recordings” folder on your device shows all audio that you’ve recorded or downloaded from the cloud.

Version 4.2.20260823.x of Pixel Recorder widely rolls out this capability.

It follows the last update in August that introduced the new app icon, which is not yet live (along with Weather) on the Pixel Watch. Recorder will also be available on Googlebooks going forward.

title: Look Out for This iPhone Duo Preorder Scam That Can Steal Your Data
snippet: Apple’s first foldable isn’t available for preorder until Oct. 16. Don’t believe anything that says otherwise.
fullText:
You can’t preorder the iPhone Duo until Oct. 16, but beware of a fake ad out there that says otherwise. Falling for it could expose a lot of personal and financial data and could even lead to theft of your cryptocurrency, if you have any.

The sleuths at Malwarebytes spotted the scam, which tries to trick people into thinking they can save $500 by preordering the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone. However, Apple has already said the Duo won’t be available for preorder until Oct. 16 and won’t go on sale in stores until Oct. 23.

The cybertheft uses the DarkSword exploit chain, which targets older iPhones that don’t have the latest security and software updates. DarkSword can compromise a device and steal data even if you simply visit a malicious web page. You don’t even need to click on or type anything to be victimized.

			

More from CNET

Malwarebytes told CNET that the iPhone Duo scam targets iPhones running iOS 18.4 to 18.6.2 and that its exploit code contained no iPad or Mac entries.

The DarkSword exploit begins as soon as the scam page loads onto your browser. The page appears legit for the most part. It’s got the Apple logo, font and language style, and there aren’t any spelling, grammar or punctuation mistakes typical of most web page scams. It’s even got an Apple copyright at the bottom. But, as Malwarebytes points out, the privacy, terms and sales policy links go nowhere.

This scam page uses Apple’s font and style to trick users into thinking it’s legitimate.Malwarebytes

Clicking the “Claim $500 Voucher” button takes you to a submission form with a few telltale indicators that it’s a scam, according to Malwarebytes. The finish color menu lists natural titanium, although the iPhone Duo only comes in star white and night sky. The form also lists size options of 6.3 and 6.9 inches, which are incorrect — the phone is 7.6 inches unfolded and 5.4 inches folded.

Filling out the form is meaningless, Malwarebytes said. If you do fill it out and submit it by clicking on the blue button, you’ll get a “Pre-Order Successful” message. By that time, however, the data theft on your iPhone has already begun.  

This info submission page helps kick off the data theft scam.Malwarebytes

The payload — the malicious code that does the stealing — goes after your passwords, messages, call history, contacts, voicemail, email, photos, app info, cryptocurrency wallet data and Apple Notes.

If you’re using a browser other than Safari, the default browser on Apple devices, a “Browser Restricted” page will direct you to open Safari, which DarkSword uses to infiltrate the device. If it can get past the iPhone’s security protections, it will begin stealing data.

How to avoid this scam

Apple says that devices running the latest versions of iOS 15 through iOS 26 are already protected. To make sure your iPhone is running the latest iOS update, go to Settings > General > Software Update. If your phone allows, install the most updated version of iOS 26 (with iOS 27 coming soon). While you’re there, also turn on Automatic Updates. An Apple support page gives more details on how to protect your iPhone from web attacks.

Also, if you’re interested in iPhone Duo preorders, only go to Apple’s official store website or other reputable online stores, such as Best Buy or your cellphone carrier. (We have a handy list here.) Don’t be tempted by ads, texts or social media posts that offer preorder deals and ask you to click a suspicious URL.

Tech companies must fix security flaws quickly, as Apple has done with DarkSword, but users must also do their part, said Stefan Dasic, a senior malware research engineer at Malwarebytes.

“We live in a time where staying safe means keeping up with technology,” Dasic told CNET. “Skipping a security update is like being handed a free replacement for a front-door lock that burglars already know how to pick, and leaving it in the box.”

Read more: 5 iPhone Duo Features I’m Already Dying to Try

If you accidentally clicked…

OK, stuff happens. If you fell victim to this scam, update your iPhone, then restart it. Malwarebytes said the data-stealing payload does not return after the phone is rebooted. There’s nothing you can do about data that was stolen before the reboot.

Malwarebytes listed several other things to do. If you have a cryptocurrency wallet on your iPhone, create a new one with a new recovery phrase and move the funds to it. If you have a crypto exchange account, secure it and contact the exchange.

Read more: A Reality Check From a Fold-aholic

Change passwords that might have been stolen. Go to a trusted device and change passwords for your email accounts, Apple account and banking, crypto and other financial accounts. And activate two-factor authentication or even more than two factors.

Scam Guard and Browser Guard, both available from Malwarebytes — a cybersecurity suite highly rated by CNET — can spot scammy screenshots and links and block fake webpages from appearing on your internet browser.

title: It’s not just you, Spotify is down in partial outage this morning
snippet: A partial outage has left the Spotify app in shambles, with core functions not working for many users. more…
fullText:
A partial outage has left the Spotify app in shambles, with core functions not working for many users.

Around 10am ET/7am PT this morning, a huge wave of Spotify users started reporting problems with the music streaming app. This includes a huge vertical spike in reports on DownDetector, as well as reports across social media.

Update: Spotify has confirmed it is aware of the outage and investigating.

We’re aware of some issues right now and are checking them out!

— Spotify Status (@SpotifyStatus) September 29, 2026

Those affected report that search and other functions are inaccessible with a “Something went wrong” error message appearing. 

	

Ironically, it’s ongoing music playback that seems to be affected least. Searching for new tracks or accessing playlists that aren’t downloaded to your device might not work, but playback seems to be working just fine – at least for now. Whether or not you can start playback will determine just how much this partial outage affects you. 

Other features such as Spotify Connect are also impacted. Some reports of the app logging users out have also surfaced, with those users unable to sign back into the app.

title: DoorDash now lets you order by text in Apple Messages
snippet: DoorDash today launched a new way to order your next meal: via text in Apple’s Messages app, powered by AI. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
DoorDash today launched a new way to order your next meal: via text in Apple’s Messages app, powered by AI. Here are the details.

DoorDash text ordering launches on iPhone, powered by AI agent

AI agents are here to stay, and they don’t just look like cute digital creatures. While Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have gotten a lot of attention, AI agents are popping up in ways that are less obviously “AI” too.

For example, today DoorDash launched the ability to skip the app and simply text to place your food order in Apple’s Messages app. It’s available in the US only to start, and interested users will need to first join this waitlist. And it’s all powered by an AI agent.

Here’s the rundown on how it works, via DoorDash’s announcement:

Text what you’re craving: Ask for a specific dish, request a local recommendation based on your mood, or simply reorder your go-to Friday night meal for the family.

Skip the search: DoorDash searches local spots, scans menus, and suggests a cart based on what you’re in the mood for. It even texts you photos of the food it recommends right from the restaurant’s store page on the DoorDash app. 

Truly personalized ordering: Text “order my usual” and it knows you mean your Friday night order — no need to spell out the dish, the modifiers, or the restaurant. It already knows whether you skip cilantro, always add extra sauce, or never miss dessert. The more you order, the more it learns, and if you want, it can message you proactively to ask if you want your usual coffee order based on your daily habits.

Manage group preferences with ease: Ordering for large groups is never easy, especially when everyone wants something different. It can handle mixed dietary preferences and different quantities in one order, so you’re not the one juggling everyone’s requests.

Checkout without ever opening the app: Confirm your order right inside the text thread and it manages checkout.

To get started, join DoorDash’s waitlist and you’ll be notified when text access is granted. Depending on demand, that access might arrive right away, or it may take some time.

Are you interested in using DoorDash’s AI agent to order via Apple’s Messages app? Let us know in the comments.

fullText:
The Wing Hummingbird 7000W-B delivery drone weighs less than 15 pounds. It has 16 propellers — four for horizontal movement and 12 for vertical — a top speed of 60 miles per hour, a carrying capacity of up to 2.7 pounds, and a delivery radius of about six miles. It is authorized by the FAA for beyond-line-of-sight piloting. As a feat of engineering, it is impressive.

So far I’ve mostly used it to send people potatoes.

It all started a few Sunday mornings ago when my neighbor Will added me and a half dozen other local dads to a group chat. I only recognized a few of the numbers.

“Anyone looking for dumb stuff to entertain the kids?” he wrote, under a video of a drone lowering a blue doggie bag into his backyard. He’d discovered that we were now in the delivery range for drone service Wing’s partnership with Walmart, and could get household items dropped onto our lawns in 25 minutes. “Hopefully liquor store will get on board soon.”

Ever since I saw the video of an Amazon drone dropping a package in someone’s pool, I’ve needed to know one thing: Do you have to order drone delivery to your own yard? I raised the question in the chat.

Will, a few minutes later: “Nathan I just ordered you a potato to see if I can send to other people. 8 minutes out.”

Two minutes after that, a neighbor named Rick: “Will just want you to know you’re going to get your potato first.”

Rick and Will had each scanned the list of deliverable items — over two thousand of them — and independently arrived at the same conclusion. “There is currently an air strike squadron of potatoes headed to our neighborhood,” Rick wrote.

At 12:14PM, a drone dropped a doggie bag in my yard. It contained a single russet potato and a bottle of water. Three minutes later, another arrived in Will’s yard, also containing a single potato and a bottle of water. (The water bottle seems to have been added as ballast; every Wing order I’ve placed came with one.)

Someone posted “The drones are everywhere.” Those of us who hadn’t met introduced ourselves. An apparently more practical dad named Jason ordered himself a pair of gloves. Dev, who lives in the next development over, was just out of drone range and could only watch in envy. Eventually, a storm rolled in and the potato drones tapered off.

My sixth-grader turned our sky potato into oven fries; Will baked his.

The wild thing — aside from the fact that you can just order a drone delivery to someone else’s yard — is that each potato delivery cost 82 cents. Total. Each order came from the Walmart Supercenter a few miles away. Wing is absolutely losing money on this. There’s no minimum order, there’s no delivery fee, and the prices are the same as in-store. Wing’s not even collecting sales tax. Welcome back, millennial lifestyle subsidy!

At these prices, if you’re not using drones to send potatoes to your neighbors you’re leaving money on the table. That evening, I remembered that my friend Bill had been going through a rough time lately.

I sent him a potato.

Okay, technically, Wing’s terms of service state “You will not use the Service to engage in any unlawful behavior, or to cause harassment, nuisance, annoyance or inconvenience to Wing, its users or any other person.” And I can definitely see ways you could abuse the system to do that.

While I lacked actual permission to land a drone potato in Bill’s yard, based on our relationship, I was confident I had spiritual permission. (This was confirmed a couple of days later when he asked me to drone deliver some candy for his kids. I sent the candy, and then another potato, and then the link to the Wing app.)

So what’s stopping someone from using this to harass people, beyond your own moral compass and the fact that they ask you not to? When I asked what safeguards the company had in place to prevent unauthorized deliveries, Wing spokesperson Jessie Poole-Strang wrote:

Wing has safely completed over 1 million residential drone deliveries, averaging thousands per day. Customers must be physically present for their first order, and every order requires a verified account and confirmation of a clear delivery zone. Just like traditional delivery or mailing a package, customers can choose to send an order to a friend or family member’s address that lives in eligible service areas. In the rare event a resident ever has a concern about a delivery to their property, our support team can help (support@wing.com).

Now, is drone delivery wasteful? If you’re only buying a single lightweight item — like a stick of deodorant, a bottle of sunscreen, or a potato — it seems more environmentally friendly than driving to the store. And as long as it’s subsidized, it’s way cheaper than DoorDash or whatever people use. I could see situations where it would be genuinely useful, especially if you can’t leave the house but you desperately need a bottle of ibuprofen and a Gatorade (for example). And of course it would be preposterous to DoorDash someone a single raw potato.

Of course, once you order more than a pound or so of stuff, that math goes off the rails. One afternoon, my wife ordered a box of frozen horchata mochi and a pint of gelato — among the few frozen desserts on the list. They arrived in two separate drones, three minutes apart, and each came with a small bottle of water. They held up surprisingly well during their 7-minute trips in the full Texas sun, considering the total lack of insulation. But it did feel silly to get two drones for two items.

That’s how they get you, of course. They hook you with convenience while hiding the true cost of the service. Drone delivery further squeezes gig workers in an already shrinking labor market, and it’s one more excuse for big companies to suppress wages. You don’t have to pay a drone, and you don’t have to tip it, either.

It’s been just over three weeks since we found out we had access to subsidized drone delivery. Aside from the two desserts and a couple of bags of gummy Nerds clusters, I’ve only used it to send potatoes to the dads. I sent three last week, plus one to myself to throw them off the scent. I’ve probably blown my cover now.

The other day someone — not me — escalated and sent Rick a broccoli potato soup. I’m pretty sure it was Will.

What have I learned from all of this? Well, I now know a few more people in my neighborhood. I’ve learned that drone delivery is way more useful to me than agentic AI has ever been. And that given the opportunity to airdrop subsidized potatoes to my friends, I’ll take it.

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

Nathan Edwards

The Wing Hummingbird 7000W-B delivery drone weighs less than 15 pounds. It has 16 propellers — four for horizontal movement and 12 for vertical — a top speed of 60 miles per hour, a carrying capacity of up to 2.7 pounds, and a delivery radius of about six miles. It is authorized by the FAA for beyond-line-of-sight piloting. As a feat of engineering, it is impressive.

So far I’ve mostly used it to send people potatoes.

title: Apple Sports adds real-time Grand Slam draws, expands soccer coverage
snippet: This week, Apple continued the steady expansion of its Apple Sports app, broadening its soccer coverage while also giving tennis fans a new way to follow some of the most important tournaments. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
This week, Apple continued the steady expansion of its Apple Sports app, broadening its soccer coverage while also giving tennis fans a new way to follow some of the most important tournaments. Here’s what’s new.

Apple Sports adds soccer leagues and tennis brackets

When Apple first released the Apple Sports app, it offered a rather limited experience, both in terms of availability and which sports it actually covered.

Since then, the app has evolved on both fronts, expanding to more than 170 countries and regions while steadily adding support for new sports, leagues, and tournaments.

Earlier this year, for instance, Apple Sports reached 90 new countries and also introduced several features around the FIFA World Cup.

This week, Apple Sports was updated once again, adding the Australian A-League Men, Egyptian Premier League, Israeli Premier League, and South African Premiership to its soccer lineup.

Additionally, the app now lets tennis fans “follow tournament draws in real-time […], with brackets for Grand Slams and 1000-level tournaments,” says Apple, adding that users can “see matchups and results at a glance for each round.”

Here are the full release notes for Apple Sports 4.4:

The soccer lineup continues to grow, with Australian A-League Men, Egyptian Premier League, Israeli Premier League, and South African Premiership.

Tennis fans can follow tournament draws in real-time on Apple Sports, with brackets for Grand Slams and 1000-level tournaments. See matchups and results at a glance for each round.

title: Gemini app starts rolling out big side panel simplification, settings redesign
snippet: The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation. more…
fullText:
The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation.

There are no major changes to the homepage, with the first differences found in the side panel. Search has moved to the top-right corner, while the chat history now offers filters: All, Ready, Needs attention, and In progress.

“Scheduled” is a new item in the list and replaces the “Scheduled actions” page. You get “Suggested” prompts like Create a news digest or Build a study quiz.

“Customize” is the big update today. The “Discover” tab surfaces skills, which are replacing Gems, and third-party connected apps. Notably, skills are activated using the ‘@’ symbol instead of a forward slash like in Gemini Spark. This page feels like a mini-app store for Gemini.

	

Meanwhile, the “Connectors” tab serves as a modernized “Connected Apps” page. Gemini is leaning into that app store parlance with the ability to “Uninstall” from the overflow menu.

Meanwhile, Gemini is getting a much-needed Settings redesign when you tap your profile avatar in the top-right corner or the gear icon. Manage account and Usage limits make up the first grouping, followed by:

Preferences: Notifications, Personal Intelligence, Avatar, Gem manager, Theme, Voice, Media, Device controls, Gemini Notebook

Data & privacy: Import memory, Contact info from your devices, Gemini Apps Activity, Your public links, Privacy Help Hub

Support: Help, Report a problem, About, Updates 

This redesign is not yet widely rolled out and only appearing on one of our Google Accounts. That said, it’s appearing on both Android and iOS.

title: Google says Chromebook updates end in 2034, ‘many’ models move to Googlebook OS
snippet: As Googlebook arrives, Google is offering a bit more information on what Chromebook owners can expect going forward. more…
fullText:
As Googlebook arrives, Google is offering a bit more information on what Chromebook owners can expect going forward.

Google has said that Chromebook updates will continue in the Googlebook era, while some models will also be eligible for upgrades. On a support page, Google provides a bit more detail.

Starting with Chromebook updates, Google says that “Chromebooks you have today will continue to receive updates through their supported lifetime,” with all Enterprise and Education management capabilities remaining in place as well:

We will maintain support for current Chromebook devices running ChromeOS as outlined in our Auto Update policy and the Chromebooks you have today will continue to receive updates through their supported lifetime. Chromebooks remain available for all school and enterprise deployments today.

Your active ChromeOS Enterprise Upgrade and ChromeOS Education Upgrade associated with existing devices will remain and maintain their current management capabilities.

Google adds that similar management tools will be coming to Googlebook, but they’re not available yet. Apparently they’re planned for the second half of 2027. Meanwhile, Google says that “many” existing Chromebook models will be eligible to transition from ChromeOS to Googlebook OS. More details are coming “soon.” A later note specifies that Google is referring to “newer commercial Chromebook models.”

	

Many of our newest Chromebook devices will be eligible to transition over to Googlebook OS. Details on migration paths and device eligibility will be shared soon.

We are working to deliver a comprehensive management experience for Googlebooks which will start rolling out in the second half of 2027.

Notably, Google specifies a year when ChromeOS updates will come to an end in a later note – 2034. Chromebooks with a 10-year update policy that extends past 2034 will be eligible to move to Googlebook OS.

ChromeOS devices will continue to receive regular updates and security patches through mid-2034. For qualifying devices purchased today whose 10-year support lifecycle extends beyond 2034, Google is committed to supporting your transition to Googlebook OS, with many devices offering direct migration paths.

This 2034 date was previously mentioned in a court case as the time when Google would “phase out” ChromeOS.

	

Finally, in regards to apps, Google says that it is “committed” to web developers despite an increased focus on Android apps on Googlebooks.

Googlebook pre-orders are open now, with models shipping in early October.

title: Cycle-Tracking Apps Bring Substantial Risks to Users, Says New Analysis
snippet: This includes apps that promote the practice of cycle syncing.
fullText:
It’s been estimated that about 50 million people worldwide use apps to track their menstrual cycles, associated mental and physical symptoms, fertility and pregnancy. However, a new analysis published in the peer-reviewed medical journal The BMJ on Wednesday argues that the risks associated with these apps and other digital cycle-tracking tools on the femtech market do more harm than good. 

The authors of the article say that these risks extend to digital menstrual cycle-tracking tools that promote “cycle syncing,” which is when one bases their diet, exercise and other lifestyle habits on their menstrual cycle phases. 

“We hope that people understand a lot of the big, splashy claims around cycle tracking and cycle syncing that people encounter on social media or in fitness or wellness spaces are not based on scientific evidence,” Katharine Lee, one of the article’s authors and an assistant professor in Tulane University’s Department of Anthropology, told CNET in an email. 

			

More from CNET

The health risks

Drawing on several studies, the analysis states that sports science research has shown there is no way to generalize about how different menstrual cycle phases affect health, performance or injury risk. These correlations are highly individual. The same goes for research on how diet can reduce cycle symptoms or improve performance, which is generally inconclusive or speculative.  

Even if these cycle connections did exist, the article argues that digital cycle-tracking tools wouldn’t be able to predict them. Apps tend to rely on a user’s self-reported menstrual bleeding date to estimate ovulation, the fertile window and future menstrual cycle phases. Without actually measuring someone’s hormones, these estimates can be imprecise, especially considering that hormones and ovulation fluctuate.

Digital menstrual cycle trackers also can’t diagnose menstrual disorders or uncover the causes of painful periods. 

“You should work with trusted health professionals if you have concerns — and yes, I know that many people struggle to get their doctors to listen to them about their periods,” Lee said. “People may want to track their cycles for any number of reasons, but a lot of digital tracking apps are no fancier than counting and averaging your data.”

When relying on these apps, there’s a risk that users may downplay health concerns as simply effects of their cycle. Or forgo established diet, exercise and sleep guidelines in the name of cycle syncing. 

Privacy isn’t the only concern when using an app to track your cycle.SeventyFour/Getty Images

The privacy problem

There’s also privacy to consider, as some apps allow third-party tracking, don’t publish transparency reports, don’t allow straightforward data deletion and don’t use local data storage, which makes it easier for them to sell data, share it with third parties or be exposed to a data breach. This is especially dangerous in areas where abortion is criminalized or where there is more gender or sex-based discrimination.

While no specific apps or tools were mentioned in this analysis, Lee said that several of the cited references focus on the policies or functionality of specific apps. 

Magnifying gender inequities

Despite being used by and promoted to millions, the article states that evidence supporting these tools’ ability to help manage people’s menstrual cycles and overall health is lacking. 

These apps also aren’t the solution to gender inequities in healthcare or in the world as a whole. Instead, they put people’s health and privacy at risk while wasting their time and compounding existing inequities around access to safety, rest, nutrition, healthcare and menstrual supplies. This is especially poignant considering that many cycle-tracking apps use the language of women’s empowerment in their marketing. 

How should you track your cycle?

There’s no single best way to track your cycle, especially since tracking methods should be tailored to individual concerns. 

For instance, according to Lee, if someone is concerned about fertility, they should ensure they track signs of ovulation, including basal body temperature, cervical mucus consistency and luteinizing hormone levels. When managing health conditions such as endometriosis, migraines or premenopausal dysphoric disorder, which can vary with menstrual cycles, monitoring the associated symptoms and predicting the next estimated time of bleeding may be more important than focusing on ovulation. 

“Most apps can’t detect ovulation or determine what phase someone is in based just on bleeding,” Lee said. “Even if these simple apps could detect ovulation and cycle phase, there are no generalizable trends in what people experience across the cycle.”

If you choose to track your cycle with an app, make sure you look into its privacy policy. Lee specifically shared research conducted by the nonprofit Mozilla Foundation, which aims to build a better tech future, and by Privacy International, a London-based charity focused on worldwide privacy protection. You could also use your digital calendar or avoid digital tracking entirely by opting for a pen and paper.

“It’s really important that people understand the potential risks [of digital menstrual tracking], including the possibility of reproductive coercion and if you live somewhere where abortion is criminalized,” Lee said. “It’s already gross enough that some apps share period data with companies to send you targeted advertising, but the safety of your information can be a real concern for many people.”

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Anna Gragert

Over the past 12 years, Anna has also written for the LA Times, Elle, Bust Magazine, Dazed, Apartment Therapy, Well+Good and more. At CNET, she's a senior editor on the Healthy Home team, and her coverage includes health, wellness tech, meal kits and home and kitchen tech with a focus on the technology that aims to help us live our healthiest, happiest lives.

title: Apple Pay finally launches in India after years on the sidelines
snippet: Some of India's largest banks are holding off on supporting Apple Pay initially.
fullText:
Apple began rolling out Apple Pay in India on Tuesday, as TechCrunch was first to report. Its first banking partner is Axis Bank, the country’s third-largest private-sector lender. The move brings the company’s payments service to the world’s most populous country after years of delays in a market dominated by the state-backed United Payments Interface (UPI).

The initial rollout is limited. Apple Pay supports eligible Axis Bank cards on Visa and Mastercard, but not India’s homegrown RuPay network. Acceptance will also be restricted to merchants and payment terminals that have been enabled for the service.

Apple said the service would be accepted by “millions of merchants” across India, including Blinkit, Croma, Ixigo, Reliance brands, Tata 1mg, and Zomato. The company has worked with payment service providers including Cashfree, JusPay, Mswipe, Paytm, PayU, Pine Labs, Razorpay, and Worldline to enable Apple Pay acceptance.

Unlike India’s ubiquitous Unified Payments Interface (UPI) system, which lets consumers make instant bank-to-bank payments without relying on cards, Apple Pay is card-based and requires individual issuers and payment infrastructure providers to integrate with the service. This makes a broad rollout more complex. Apple’s commercial terms have also emerged as a sticking point with some of India’s largest banks, people familiar with the matter said.

Apple is seeking a fee of about 20 basis points (0.2%) on transactions, according to the people, a significant bite out of the roughly 40 to 50 basis points (0.4% to 0.5%) of margin in the payments layer. The fee structure is broadly consistent with Apple Pay’s commercial model in other markets, the people said. HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and SBI Card are not supporting Apple Pay at launch as negotiations over commercial terms continue, one of the people told TechCrunch.

Apple, Axis Bank, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and SBI Card did not respond to requests for comment on the launch. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that Apple was preparing to launch Apple Pay in India in October, starting with Axis Bank credit cards.

Apple Pay has entered a payments market that looks markedly different from the U.S. and other card-heavy economies. India’s digital payments boom has been driven largely by UPI, the state-backed system that lets consumers move money directly between bank accounts.

UPI handles the bulk of digital payments in India, where scanning a QR code to pay directly from a bank account has become commonplace. Apple Pay, by contrast, initially addresses a much smaller card payments market.

Nevertheless, Apple Pay could appeal to India’s growing base of iPhone users, who tend to be more affluent and are more likely to use premium credit cards. Those customers could make the service hard for banks to ignore, despite UPI’s dominance.

Even if Apple Pay remains a niche service, the economics could still make India meaningful for Apple. The transaction fee the iPhone maker would charge would give it another way to monetize its growing base of iPhone users in the country, the people said.

At launch, eligible Axis Bank customers can add their credit cards to Apple’s Wallet app and use Apple Pay for online purchases as well as contactless payments at supported terminals, the people said.

An Apple Pay transaction could work at a terminal operated by an independent payments provider that has enabled the service but fail at another terminal whose acquiring bank has not, one of the people said. That could make acceptance uneven during the initial rollout, even for customers with supported cards.

The launch adds another piece to Apple’s growing business in India, where it has been expanding iPhone sales, local manufacturing, and its retail footprint. Apple accounted for 28% of India’s smartphone market by value in 2025, up from 23% a year earlier, per an earlier report by Counterpoint Research.

India already accounts for about a quarter of global iPhone production, and that share could rise to 30% to 35% over the next five years, Indian English daily Business Standard reported last month, citing an Indian government official.

Update: This story, originally published Tuesday morning, has been updated to reflect that the launch is now underway.

title: Apple releases iOS 27.0.1 for iPhone, here’s what’s new
snippet: Apple has just released iOS 27.0.1, a new iPhone software update with key bug fixes for issues introduced in iOS 27. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple has just released iOS 27.0.1, a new iPhone software update with key bug fixes for issues introduced in iOS 27. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.0.1 fixes iPhone 18 Pro Face ID issue, plus includes additional bug fixes

iPhone users, Apple has just launched its latest software update. iOS 27.0.1 is now available to install via Settings ⇾ General ⇾ Software Update.

Here’s what Apple’s official release notes say:

This update provides bug fixes for your iPhone, including fixes for the following issues:

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max may unexpectedly restart when Face ID fails to authenticate

A color artifact may appear on photos captured at 2x under certain lighting conditions at f/1.48 on a small number of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max devices

Opening Notification Center and Control Center simultaneously may cause the touchscreen to become unresponsive

As 9to5Mac previously reported, some iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max users experienced crashes when Face ID was unable to properly authenticate them. Apple promised a fix was coming this week, and now it has delivered via iOS 27.0.1.

Out of the listed fixes in Apple’s release notes, only the Notification Center and Control Center issue applies to all iPhone models. 

	

But Apple’s notes aren’t typically comprehensive of all changes, so older iPhones will likely benefit from other, unmentioned bug fixes in iOS 27.0.1 too.

iOS 27 launched two weeks ago as a major new iPhone software update. As happens most years around this time, the public release brought some bugs to the surface that Apple wasn’t able to discover during beta testing, so iOS 27.0.1 fixes some of those issues.

fullText:
Apple has teamed up with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) to launch a new guide to “help families create healthy digital habits.” 

The new guide follows Apple’s launch of a range of new child safety features in iOS 27. 

Apple says this new guide is meant to help families balance screen time with sleep, exercise, schoolwork, and socialization. 

The guide includes a six-step breakdown for families, per Apple: 

Start a conversation about screen time, with tips for parents to approach the topic and establish expectations in a way that helps kids feel included in the plan.

Create a Child Account, which enables age-based safeguards and gives parents access to parental controls to manage their child’s experience.

Set safety settings for websites and apps, including Ask to Buy and Ask to Browse, so families can review new apps and websites together.

Make a schedule for device use, using Time Allowances and Schedules to balance time online with sleep, schoolwork, physical activity, and time with family and friends.

Manage communications, with parents deciding who their child can communicate with and Communication Safety, on by default for all users under 18, helping protect kids from viewing or sharing sensitive content.

Continue the conversation as kids grow, with guidance on adjusting the family’s plan over time.

You can find the new guide, “Building Healthy Digital Habits: A Guide for Families,” on Apple’s website.

title: Instagram partner schools can now post content only their students can view
snippet: Meta last year launched a school partnership program for Instagram, in which it promised to prioritize student reports of cyberbullying. The company has now expanded the program to allow schools to post stories and notes that only their own students can view – alongside support for clubs, teams, and more … more…
fullText:
Meta last year launched a school partnership program for Instagram, in which it promised to prioritize student reports of cyberbullying.

The company has now expanded the program to allow schools to post stories and notes that only their own students can view – alongside support for clubs, teams, and more …

Instagram School Partnership Program

Instagram is a platform that doesn’t exactly have the best of track records when it comes to teenage mental health. Even the company’s own internal research showed that Instagram could be harmful to as many as 20% of teenage girls using the apps by increasing anxieties about physical attractiveness and popularity, among other things.

Cyberbullying has been another significant problem for teen users of social networks, and Meta last year launched a program intended to help schools tackle the issue. When schools signed up to its partnership program, Meta promised that reports filed by students and staff would be prioritized.

Reports submitted by school partners that may violate Instagram’s Community Standards will be prioritized for review. Schools will also receive status updates on the reports and notifications as soon as Instagram takes action on the report.

New school features

Meta says it is today adding a number of new features to the program.

Channels. These allow schools to share updates to parents and students. Only school administrators can post messages in channels.

School Stories and notes. Both staff and students can post these, and they will only be visible by verified students at the school. School administrators can remove posts.

Clubs and Teams. Anyone in the school can create clubs and teams to act as a central hub for communicating relevant events and information.

Student directory. Students can access a directory of other students at their school on the platform. This is visible only to other students and teen followers they follow back.

Meta says that the new features are intended for use outside of classroom hours, noting that teen accounts allow parents to block usage during school hours.

Verification of high school students is carried out by UNiDAYS, the same company Apple uses to allow access to educational pricing.

title: Microsoft launches 12-inch Surface Pro with Snapdragon X2 Plus & 5G, 13-inch Surface Laptop too
snippet: Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149. more…
fullText:
Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149.

The Surface Laptop and Surface Pro both picked up their Snapdragon X2 upgrades back in June, but that left the smaller models waiting on refreshes. As a part of Snapdragon Summit, Microsoft is confirming that those will arrive on October 13.

Surface Pro 12-inch is getting a Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, a 25% brighter display, and a battery that’s “30% more efficient.” There’s an optional 5G model coming too, which Microsoft says was “one of the most requested additions.” All models now include either 16GB or 24GB of RAM, removing the 8GB option on last year’s model, with either 256GB or 512GB of storage. 

It’s mostly the same tablet otherwise, just now with a starting price of $1,149. That’s $300 more than the base model sold for, and that’s after a major price hike across the whole lineup back in April. Even directly comparing the 16/256GB model, it’s still a $100 price hike. 

	

The formula is similar on Surface Laptop 13-inch, with this latest generation getting Snapdragon X2 Plus, ditching its 8GB model, and starting at $1,199 – $50 up from the last generation. Again, there are upgrades including a brigher display, but it’s nearly identical to last year’s model outside of the chipset bump.

Microsoft is also launching a new Surface Mouse which has haptic feedback and a customizable Copilot button. It costs $79.99 and will also be available on October 13. Both come with a new “Microsoft Ink Canvas” app.

fullText:
Samsung is today officially launching its new Galaxy Tab S12 series with the Tab S12+ and Tab S12 Ultra delivering big displays, powerful specs, and some new software tricks too.

Available starting October 7, the Galaxy Tab S12+ and Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra continue Samsung’s flagship tablet series with some nominal upgrades. While they’re visually almost identical to prior generations, there are some spec bumps, including the new MediaTek Dimensity 9500.

title: Gemini app replacing Gems with skills in November
snippet: In 2024, Google introduced Gems as “custom versions of Gemini.” The Gemini app will soon replace Gems with “skills.” more…
fullText:
In 2024, Google introduced Gems as “custom versions of Gemini.” The Gemini app will soon replace Gems with “skills.”

Going to the Gems manager today reveals a new notice at the top: “Gems will become skills starting Nov 17, 2026.”

Starting November 17, 2026, we’ll automatically begin migrating your Gems to skills. You will be able to use your Gems until they migrate.

Google introduced skills with Gemini Spark, and they serve the same purpose as Gems at a high level. Both let you give Gemini custom instructions.

	
	

Gems let you go a step further by setting a default tool, like Create image or Canvas, and adding specific files for context. They can also be shared with other users via links.

That said, skills are more easily invoked with a / in the prompt box, while multiple can be used at the same time. This broader access is better than first having to go to Gems in the side panel and scrolling down for My Gems.

Google’s announcement might have rolled out slightly early as the “Learn more” help article and “Create skills” button do not work yet.

If you’re a Google AI Pro or AI Ultra subscriber, you can make skills by switching to the Gemini Spark tab. Typing a slash in the Chat box will let you use skills in the main conversational experience.

title: Meta launches audio-only glasses and Gen 3 Ray-Ban with slimmer designs
snippet: Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release. more…
fullText:
Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release.

Despite public backlash in recent months, smart glasses continue to explode in popularity and, as it stands, Meta is by far the biggest player in the game. Today’s event further saw the company digging in on its smart glasses success with three new releases.

The self-branded Meta Glasses lineup is adding new styles that start at just $249. A new pair of Meta Adventurer glasses will be available with a black frame and grey lenses and a plug-in case. They’re available starting October 23. 

Next in line is a pair of audio-only glasses, Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Starting at $349 in October, these glasses ditch the camera and, in turn, also deliver a much slimmer form factor. They weigh 43g and run for 12 hours on a single charge (48 hours in the case). Meta says the new hardware features “professional-adjustable temple tips, adjustable or swappable nose pads, and overextension hinges.” 

	

Styles include “Clubmaster” and “Burbank” in a variety of frame and lens styles.

Beyond that, Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is available today starting at $449. Meta says to expect longer battery life – 9 hours, an hour longer than Gen 2 – and the same camera capabilities, including 3K video recording. The hardware is slimmer and adds professional-adjustable temple tips. 

Meta is also launching this latest generation in way more styles, with 27 combinations across “Aviator,” “Wayfarer,” and cateye “Zena” frame styles.

You can order Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) now through Meta’s store.

Finally, Meta is also upgrading its Display glasses with hands-free navigation, “Hologram” personas for video calls, new apps, notification mirroring from your phone, and Threads integration. Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are also expanding to the UK, Canada, France, Italy, and Germany, and you can finally order them online in the US, still priced at $799.

title: WhatsApp adds new parental controls for teen accounts
snippet: Parents can limit how teens use channels, whose Status they can see, who can see their Status updates, and control who can add teens to groups.
fullText:
WhatsApp is introducing new parental controls that could allow guardians to keep a tab on who their teens interact with, and also choose content settings for Meta AI chats.

With the new controls, parents can limit how teens use channels, whose Status they can see, and who can see their Status updates. Guardians can also control who can add teens to groups or who can see their profile picture. Parents can also choose to get a notification when a teen joins a new group, leaves one, or the group size grows to 30, 100, or 250 members.

All of these settings are gated behind a PIN set by parents, so if a teen needs to change anything, they would need their parents’ approval. Guardians can also turn these controls off completely.

Besides these settings, parents can also set content settings for Meta AI. There’s now an option to choose the default 13+ setting, or a stricter ‘Limited Content’ option that disables private processing-based features like incognito chat and message summaries.

WhatsApp’s new parental control screen Image Credits: WhatsAppImage Credits:WhatsApp

WhatsApp said despite these new controls, messages and calls on the app remain end-to-end encrypted, and no one can see them.

Meta has been on the receiving end of several lawsuits that accuse the company’s social media products of causing harm to children. Lawmakers have pressed Meta and, in particular, Instagram, on the company’s delays to launch teen safety features. In August, the company agreed to pay a hefty $18 billion fine to settle a lawsuit brought by 29 states in the U.S.

The company has been aggressive in introducing features to protect children across its apps. This year, it has rolled out movie rating-inspired content controls, launched parental controls for interactions with Meta AI, added pre-teen accounts on WhatsApp, and started alerting parents if their children search for self-harm content on Instagram.

title: Charter Space raises $5M to bring insurance to the stars
snippet: As Charter explains on its website, a common experience for space companies is that regular insurers "heard a bunch of scary science words and freaked out."
fullText:
Charter Space, a finalist in last year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield, has raised a $5 million seed round to keep growing its budding space insurance business.

The El Segundo, California-based startup said Wednesday it’s already servicing over 50 companies across the U.S. space and defense industrial base following the launch of its nationally-licensed insurance brokerage in May.

Insurance-focused Crystal Venture Partners led the round, and fintech investors QED and Blank Ventures, early-stage venture firm Hustle Fund, and Gaingels, an investment syndicate that backs startups with underrepresented leadership, also participated.

Things go wrong in the space industry all the time, so companies are constantly planning contingencies. But insuring objects that go to space is still a rare practice. Charter Space’s founder and CEO, Yuk Chi Chan (above, right), believes this is largely because of the high cost of underwriting something like a satellite. As Charter explains on its website, a common experience for space companies is that regular insurers “heard a bunch of scary science words and freaked out.”

When Chan started Charter Space with co-founder Yukun Yin, they set out to build a centralized software for aerospace engineering that would bring together the technical, manufacturing, and test data for customers. But he realized there was a lot of potential value in plugging that data into the underwriting process.

“We want more satellites to get insured, because that means that everything as a whole is much, much safer. If we can proliferate insurance coverage, one, that’s good for the space industrial base, a lot more companies have a safety net… But it’s also a lot healthier for the overall economy, because then that encourages global investment from different alternative capital sources,” Chan told TechCrunch last year. “You’re not solely reliant on VC or some growth equity. You can start bringing in debt, credit, lots of different options that you have in any other sort of advanced industry.”

Space companies don’t have many options for financial services because the space used to have very few players. The industry was until recently dominated by governments and defense contractors who, after the Cold War, tended to move slowly and conservatively.

But the boom of new space companies over the last decade, spurred in large part by SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket lowering the cost of launching things into orbit, means there’s now enough demand for companies like Charter Space to build and grow. There are new players making satellites and spaceships, and new launch providers competing to fill the void that SpaceX is about to leave when it retires the Falcon 9.

“Charter Space sits at the intersection of two enormous opportunities: the rapid growth of the commercial space economy and the need for a modern approach to understanding and insuring the increasingly complex risks that accompany that growth,” Jonathan Crystal, managing partner of Crystal Venture Partners, said in a statement. “Insurance is critical infrastructure for a strong and sustainable space industry, and we believe Charter Space is building the platform that will help the space economy scale safely and sustainably.”

Michael Yaworsky, the commissioner of insurance regulation in Florida, still the leading launch location in the country, said insurance is “the precondition for growth in space” and said it opens the door for more local investment. “The state that leads on insurance will be the destination for capital investing in the industries of the future, and lay the foundation for continued American greatness for the next 250 years and beyond,” he said in a statement to TechCrunch.

Charter Space has raised $8 million to date, and said it will use the proceeds of the seed round to grow its sales organization and its insurance offerings. Other products on the table include coverage for “novel mission concepts,” like space-based nuclear power, lunar missions, and in-space servicing of other spacecraft.

title: Apple faces renewed scrutiny over removal of ICEBlock from the App Store
snippet: CNN reports that Rep. Jamie Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week challenging the company’s explanation for removing ICEBlock from the App Store last year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
CNN reports that Rep. Jamie Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week challenging the company’s explanation for removing ICEBlock from the App Store last year. Here are the details.

ICEBlock removal once again under scrutiny

According to CNN, Apple sent a letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin last July explaining its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store, and Raskin has now responded with new questions about the company’s justification.

For context, ICEBlock was one of the most prominent apps that allowed users to report and track ICE activity in their area. The app rapidly rose in popularity during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, growing from around 20,000 users to roughly one million within weeks.

As its popularity skyrocketed, ICEBlock became the target of the US government, with then-Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly calling for Apple to remove the app and warning its developer that he could face prosecution.

Following pressure from the DOJ, Apple removed it and several similar apps from the App Store, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents. The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

This, in turn, prompted Raskin to investigate whether the Trump administration had pressured Apple and Google into removing ICE-tracking apps, and what impact those removals may have had on constitutionally protected speech.

As part of that investigation, CNN reports that Apple sent Raskin a letter last July explaining why it removed ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store.

From CNN:

Apple says its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar platforms from the app store last year was prompted by concerns — including those raised by the Trump administration — about agent safety following a fatal shooting that left two detainees dead at a Dallas Immigration and Customs Enforcement office.

Apple’s explanation came in a July letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, who earlier this year launched an investigation into the Justice Department’s role in the removal of the apps from Apple’s and Google’s app stores and the impact on constitutionally protected speech. The letter has not previously been reported.

CNN says that Apple’s letter to Raskin also mentioned that the company approved ICEBlock in April 2025, after developer Joshua Aaron addressed what Apple referred to as “certain user privacy concerns.”

Apple also reportedly said it continued to monitor news coverage and criticism of the app in the months that followed, ultimately deciding to remove ICEBlock and similar apps after concluding they violated its App Store guidelines by providing “precise location information about ICE officers,” which could potentially be used for targeted attacks.

Apple also cited concerns raised by Bondi after the Dallas shooting, as well as comments from FBI Director Kash Patel that the shooter had searched for apps that tracked ICE agents’ locations.

According to Apple, those concerns, together with what it described as a broader increase in ICE activity and threats against agents, prompted the company to conduct a new review of ICEBlock.

Raskin pushes back

According to CNN, Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week further questioning the company’s justification for removing ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store.

	

From CNN:

Raskin said the move suggests that Apple may be “working with the government to violate its customers’ First Amendment rights to record and report on the activities of their own government” in a response letter sent Monday to Apple’s senior director of government affairs, Timothy Powderly.

CNN also notes that Raskin disputed Apple’s reliance on the Dallas shooting, arguing that the gunman did not need an ICE-tracking app to locate a fixed government facility and reportedly found the address using “an app that comes standard on Apple devices.”

He also pointed to other navigation apps that remain available on the App Store despite providing real-time information about law enforcement locations, and asked Apple to conduct a new independent review of the removals and provide a full list of apps it removed in response to concerns raised by the DOJ.

title: Galaxy S27 Ultra’s missing camera shown in leaks is its 3x zoom
snippet: Previous Galaxy S27 Ultra leaks have directed attention to the new camera island, but don’t overlook the missing camera lens left behind with the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Apparently, that camera is the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra’s 10MP 3x zoom. more…
fullText:
Previous Galaxy S27 Ultra leaks have directed attention to the new camera island, but don’t overlook the missing camera lens left behind with the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Apparently, that camera is the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra’s 10MP 3x zoom.

We’ve seen a selection of leaks with details galore, including privacy displays, battery upgrades, and more. Any render that’s come out has shown off an entirely new camera island design, and it’s become the focus of the new phone. Love it or hate it, it’s there and almost square.

According to another leak via @UniverseIce on Twitter/X, the Galaxy S27 Ultra won’t have a 3x optical zoom lens with a 10MP sensor. Instead, the phone will have a wide 1x lens setup and a 5x optical zoom unit – 50MP, if left unchanged as suggested.

It is now confirmed that the Galaxy S27 Ultra will no longer have a 3× telephoto camera.

This means its rear camera system will jump directly from the 1× main camera to the 5× telephoto camera.

The main camera uses the ISOCELL HP6, essentially a Galaxy-customized version of the… https://t.co/qYGcdX93oy

— Ice Universe (@UniverseIce) September 29, 2026

The latest renders clearly show a missing lens if you compare the phone to last year’s model. The Galaxy S26 Ultra had a 3x and 5x optical zoom camera, totaling four sensors across the back of the phone. Now, sitting in a section of much larger real estate, the new camera array appears to have only three cameras.

	

A render posted by @OnLeaks labels portions of the new panel. Where previous renders showed another lens underneath the flash LED, this new render places the LED at the bottom, topped by additional sensors, a microphone, and what may now be the 5x zoom lens.

As is the case with nearly every Galaxy S series leak, these are to be taken with a grain of salt. Renders have come and gone, but we won’t know the final details until Samsung launches the device sometime in early 2027.

fullText:
Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

iOS 27 debuted to the public almost two weeks ago, with the flagship feature being Siri AI. While Siri AI was revolutionary compared to what existed prior, it still has some shortcomings. QuillCue aims to close one of the gaps with Siri AI by providing a custom keyboard that lets you save prompts for later.

Highlights

QuillCue is a rather great concept. Using custom keyboards on iOS, it allows you to insert fully prewritten prompts into Siri AI. Just swipe down from the top of your screen, switch over to the custom keyboard, select your prompt, and press enter.

It saves a lot of time if you have Siri questions you end up asking regularly, but don’t want to always type the same thing over and over again. One of the default prompts is finding nearby coffee shops that allow laptops for remote work. Since this is dependent on location, it’s always great to fetch new results that you might’ve not known about. 

Of course, you can pre-write any prompt that Siri AI can handle. QuillCue just saves you the hassle of having to respeak or retype it every single time, making Siri AI a lot easier to use.

If you end up writing a rather lengthy prompt full of different steps, QuillCue can save you a lot of time – since Siri AI doesn’t currently have a concept of ‘skills’ or learning from your usage. The possibilities are really endless. The app also offers folders for sorting your different prompts.

Lastly, it also offers the ability to import and export prompt libraries, so if you’d like to share prompts with friends or transfer them between devices, you can do so easily.

Download the app

QuillCue is available for free on the App Store, with no ads or in app purchases. You can follow the developer Parker Ortolani on X for updates. 

It requires an iPhone running iOS 27.0 or later, and is currently limited to users in the United States.
