title: Can Air Purifiers Clear Wildfire Smoke From Your Home? What Our Lab Data Reveals
snippet: We’ve found that some are much better at doing so than others.
fullText:
On the morning of June 7, 2023, I walked out of my Brooklyn apartment and noticed the skies were hazier than usual, but I chalked it up to a change in weather and headed to work. When I arrived at my Manhattan office that overlooked the Hudson River, though, I knew this was something very different. 

On a normal day, I’d have a clear view of New Jersey on the other side of the water, but on this day, it was merely a blur. As I inspected the thick fog, it dawned on me: This wasn’t fog at all. It was smoke from wildfires that were raging in Canada. The air quality monitor on my phone’s weather app confirmed it. 

Although there was a thick plume of smoke over the city, I could still see the blue skies peeking through, so I continued to work. But by the end of the day, the sky had turned completely dark with an ominous orange tint. This experience was a first for me, so I was alarmed about having to go back outside to return home, and I wasn’t alone, as people in my office began passing out dust masks. I wasn’t sure if they’d help much, but I took one just in case. 

			

More from CNET

Even in the subway system, the smell of smoke was undeniable. I made it home, took my dog for the shortest walk possible, then immediately went inside, opened my laptop and ordered an air purifier. I’ve had one running ever since.

The view from my office window in the morning, left, and the view from the same window at the end of the workday, right.Corin Cesaric-Epple/CNET

A perfect storm  

Although the smoke cleared relatively quickly, and the New York skyline bounced back after two days, not every area is as lucky. Texas and the West Coast are particularly vulnerable to these recurring disasters due to their dry climates and the intensifying effects of climate change. Similarly, the 2023 Canadian wildfires occurred during the country’s driest period since 1980, according to NASA.

Data from the National Interagency Fire Center underscores the increasing threat of wildfires. There were 64,897 wildfires in 2024, a sharp increase compared with 77,850 in 2025. Rising temperatures, reduced rainfall and earlier snowmelt around the world create the ideal setting for wildfires to run rampant. 

These types of statistics can feel overwhelming, and while you largely can’t stop a wildfire from happening, you do have control over the air you breathe indoors. To see if air purifiers can make your home’s air safer and cleaner during wildfire season, we tested more than a dozen models to find out.

Key takeaways: 

According to our exclusive lab data, air purifiers can help clear smoke from a home, but some do significantly better than others.

After testing 18 air purifiers, the Coway 450 was the best overall in our 2026 tests. It had the best overall average results in our particle-removal test and received an Editors’ Choice award.

The Coway 400S was selected as the best air purifier for wildfire smoke because it cleared T90 fine particles in 39 seconds on high fan, earning it a CNET Lab Test award for that performance.

	

			

	

			

									

						Best Air Purifiers of 2026					

							

		

What our testing revealed

To conduct our particle-removal tests at our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, our technicians built a custom smoke chamber to test how quickly an air purifier can remove particulate matter from the air. They created a homemade smoke bomb made from potassium nitrate (KNO3), sucrose (sugar) and sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), then placed it in the smoke chamber along with the unit being tested and a particle counter. 

This test showcases how well each air purifier works at clearing both coarse and fine particles. When determining which unit is best for wildfire smoke, we paid close attention to the fine-particle result, since, according to AirNow, “approximately 90% of total particle mass emitted from wildfires consists of fine particles.”

Fine particles are also the most detrimental to human health because they are tiny, less than or equal to 2.5 microns, so when they are inhaled, they can embed deep into your lungs and cause numerous health issues. 

Our lab data revealed that two Coway air purifiers and one Dreame air purifier especially excelled at clearing fine particles.

The Coway 400S is our top pick for clearing smoke from your home because of its exceptional performance at high fan speed. In our 2026 test, it cleared T90 (the time it took for 90% of particles to be removed) fine particles on high fan in just 39 seconds.

The Coway 450, CNET’s choice for best overall air purifier of 2026, was close to matching the 400S’s performance on high fan, but outperformed it on low fan, taking 1 minute and 53 seconds to remove T90 fine particles.

However, the Dreame Furcatch was the top performer in terms of low fan performance. It cleared T90 fine particles on low fan in 1 minute and 24 seconds, winning a CNET Lab Test award in the process. But it did not perform nearly as well as the Coway options above when set to high fan.

While all three models are great options for different reasons, your choice ultimately depends on how you plan to use the air purifier. 

If you need quick bursts at high fan speed in the event of sudden smoke, go with the Coway 400S. If you prefer a unit that does particularly well on low fan and you plan to always keep it on that setting, opt for the Dreame Furcatch. For the most consistent performance at both high and low fan speeds, the Coway 450 is the best option.

In addition to our particle-removal tests, we also tested energy usage and loudness. The Dyson HushJet earned two CNET Lab Test awards for being the quietest and most energy-efficient option on our list. 

From left to right, the Dreame Furcatch, the Coway 450 and the Levoit 200S-P, three winners from our 2026 air purifier testing. Zooey Liao/CNET/Coway/Dreame/Levoit

Air purifier use in real life

CNET’s wellness editor, Anna Gragert, has experienced wildfires firsthand. In 2025, California’s Eaton Fire forced her to evacuate her apartment, but luckily, it stopped five miles short of her home.

“Despite taping up our window seams before deciding to evacuate, we returned to an apartment that smelled of smoke, and everything was covered in a thin layer of ash,” Gragert says. “We relied on two air purifiers to filter the air and remove the smoke smell, and wouldn’t have been able to comfortably live in our apartment without them after experiencing a wildfire so close to home.”

While an air purifier won’t protect your home from a wildfire and you should always pay close attention to evacuation orders in your area, it can provide an important line of defense if smoke hits your city so you can breathe easier, both figuratively and literally.

When I arrived at my Manhattan office that overlooked the Hudson River, though, I knew this was something very different.

On a normal day, I’d have a clear view of New Jersey on the other side of the water, but on this day, it was merely a blur. As I inspected the thick fog, it dawned on me: This wasn’t fog at all. It was smoke from wildfires that were raging in Canada. The air quality monitor on my phone’s weather app confirmed it.

title: I Visited Lightship’s AE.1 EV Travel Trailer, and Now I Want to Take an Off-the-Grid Road Trip
snippet: The company, founded by Tesla veterans, is expanding manufacturing in Colorado to keep up with demand from RV enthusiasts.
fullText:
I’m approaching the age where I’m supposed to start desiring RV life. I’m not planning to retire anytime soon, but the older I get, the more appealing the idea of abandoning yard work, home repairs and geographic permanence for a life on the open road in a big old house on wheels becomes. My neighbors have an RV they park in the space between our houses, keeping both a permanent location and a home they can travel in; they still have yard work and house repairs, but few complaints.

So it was with some curiosity that I visited a pop-up for Lightship, a Colorado company making EV trailers for RV enthusiasts, outside the flagship Yeti outdoor-recreation store in Austin, Texas. The company’s eye-catching AE.1 trailer was parked and open to the public. (AE.1 refers to Aero-Electric 1.)

The Lightspeed AE.1 includes lots of modern design touches, like a kitchen area with a two-burner stove, a fridge and freezer, microwave and a hidden compact dishwasher.Omar L. Gallaga for CNET

Lightship staffers handed out brochures, stickers and pins to visitors who climbed into the trailer, some of whom seemed surprised by the sleek, air-conditioned interior. The demo model boasted a cushioned lounge area, appliances including a hideaway dishwasher, microwave, full sink and stovetop, a full bathroom and shower area, and plenty of storage. It can sleep up to six.

			

More from CNET

The selling point of the highly customizable AE.1, which starts at $157,500, is that it offers a more modern design than most RVs and trailers. It includes thoughtful design touches and an electric-powered motor called TrekDrive that kicks in when in motion to lighten the load on whatever’s pulling the trailer. If it’s an EV truck or SUV, that could significantly extend the range between charges.

Pushing back on decades of RV design

Ben Parker, Lightship’s co-founder and chief product officer, worked at Tesla in California as a battery engineer and was inspired while traveling in an RV during the pandemic. Parker started the company with Toby Krauss, another former Tesla employee who worked in finance and product management and serves as Lightspeed’s CEO.

Parker said there’s a gigantic market of Americans who want to travel in camper RVs, but their options have been limited to a few highly consolidated manufacturers offering unchanging designs. So far, he said, customers interested in Lightship are a mix of EV owners and longtime enthusiasts who want “greater capacity, comfort and independence.”

“Our customers are people who love spending time outdoors and want more freedom in how they travel,” Parker said.

Ben Parker, chief product officer and co-founder of Lightship, stands next to the company’s AE.1 EV camper trailer at a pop-up event in Austin, Texas on Sept. 26, 2026.Omar L. Gallaga for CNET

The AE.1’s most notable design feature is that it compresses from a 10-foot-tall Camp Mode with lots of windows and headroom to a Road Mode that lowers the roof to under 7 feet, making the AE.1 more aerodynamic in motion. Most of the trailer’s features, from the lighting to extras like an auto-leveling system and a motorized awning, are controlled by an app. A solar array on the trailer’s roof helps keep power flowing. 

If you limit your A/C and power use, the AE.1 can last for about a week off the grid before it needs additional charging, Parker said. The AE.1 has hookups for EV charging as well as the kind of 220-volt hookups found at RV parks. It can hook up to external devices with vehicle-to-load power capabilities.

Some of the more interesting option features include a pull-down bed that attaches to the trailer’s ceiling and a setup for a 4K video projector that can be mounted inside the trailer for viewing on a pull-down screen. 

“The demand we’ve seen reflects a broader appetite for innovation in the RV space,” Parker said. “Customers are excited by the idea of an RV that combines modern technology, energy independence and a dramatically improved towing experience in a single product.”

The co-founder said his company wants the buying and using experience of an AE.1 to wow customers enough for Lightship to gain a foothold in a market that’s not very open to newcomers.

“Breaking into any established industry requires earning trust,” he said. “We’ve focused on building a high-quality product that solves real customer pain points and delivering an experience that people can immediately appreciate once they see it and use it for themselves.”

New trailer players

Lightship is headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. It’s expanding its manufacturing center there to accommodate additional trailer production, as well as production of a carriage-minus-trailer product called PowerSled, which it’s been selling to businesses like movie productions that need a mobile platform with electric power.

Lightship’s mission to disrupt the RV market is not unlike that of another company, Pebble, that has also been making EV trailers in California.

Parker said the main difference between Lightship and Pebble is that Lightship is sourcing more of its materials domestically. Parker estimates that about 75% of the materials used to make an AE.1 are sourced domestically, and all assembly is done in-house.

Pebble, however, is undercutting Lightship on price. Lightship originally planned to offer a lower-priced $125,000 base model without the self-propelled TrekDrive motor. However, the company has since changed its strategy, moving to a single standard base price with a standard 77 kWh battery and various add-on options and upgrades.

Possible retirement plans

For me, a non-RV person, the AE.1 feels design-forward and includes features like a built-in auto-hitch, an auto-leveler, and lots of charging ports and stations, all of which appeal to someone like me who has no idea what they’re doing. The interior feels spacious, but not so much that it makes the exterior look oversized. The ability to shrink down to a smaller size — the AE.1 performs safety checks before compressing to ensure windows aren’t open and nothing will break — brings the wow factor.

It doesn’t take much time in the trailer to imagine traveling in it and using Lightspeed’s trailer as a mobile workstation (satellite internet service is not included, but it can be hooked up).

The AE.1 isn’t cheap, but it might be worth putting on the retirement wish list. You will still have to wait: the company’s waitlist for delivery is currently about a year long.

Lightspeed began shipping AE.1 trailers last year and said it’s producing about 30 per month for the rest of this year. By sometime in 2027, with its expanded factory floor, it plans to ramp that up to 40 per month.

If you want to check out the AE.1 for yourself, the company maintains showrooms north of Denver and in San Francisco and will host a pop-up event in Las Vegas in late November.

He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Simplifies Streaming Options, and I Went Hands-On
snippet: The 2026 streamer from Amazon features a new remote and support for HDR10 and Samsung’s HDR10 Plus.
fullText:
Amazon has unveiled a new Fire TV Stick 4K as part of a simplified lineup for the popular streamers, and it has 4K HDR10 playback.

The $60 Fire TV Stick 4K, which replaces both the Fire TV Stick 4K Select and 4K Plus, comes with a new remote and support for HDR10 and Samsung’s HDR10 Plus. It has 8GB internal storage, a quad-core 1.7 GHz processor and support for Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.3 and Bluetooth Low Energy. The company says the Stick 4K is 20% to 40% faster than the similarly priced Roku Streaming Stick Plus.

While it’s not consequential, as it’s going to spend all of its time behind your TV, the Fire TV Stick 4K feels solid in the hand. It seems much more luxe than any other Fire TV Stick I’ve ever used. The device comes with a USB cable, and it no longer needs to be plugged into the wall; it can be powered by your TV’s USB port.

			

More from CNET

The new remote no longer has a dedicated Alexa button.

I found the “upgraded” experience extends to the redesigned remote, which, unusually, no longer includes a prominent blue Alexa button. Instead, the most obvious button features a bright red home icon, and the microphone is now relegated to the top right.

Amazon also said that a new premium remote is coming in 2027, which features backlighting and a “find my remote” feature.

The streaming device is designed to be used in conjunction with Alexa Plus, and one impressive feature the representatives showed me was the forthcoming ability to plug articles into the app. They showed me how to load a “10 best movies about…” article into the Fire TV app and have the TV add the movies listed to a watch-next list.

The Fire TV Stick 4K home screenTy Pendlebury/CNET

In general, the setup and use of the Fire TV Stick 4K felt very familiar, but since it was fresh out of the box, I didn’t notice any blazing speeds. This will likely improve over time as the device learns the apps I use most.

The best part about the Fire TV Stick 4K’s release, however, is the simplification of the range for buyers, and this stick should now be the go-to device for most people. Enthusiasts who want to make the most of their home cinema should get the $85 4K Max model for Dolby Vision and Atmos, or support for add-on speakers via Alexa Home Theater.

The range is now just four main devices:

Fire TV Stick HD $40

Fire TV Stick 4K $60

Fire TV Stick 4K Max $85

Fire TV Cube $199

The Fire TV Stick 4K is available now for an introductory price of $30, and this will likely continue until Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week.

title: This Might Be the Only Hair Straightening Tool You Need
snippet: It’s super lightweight and delivers more impressive results than you’d expect for its size.
fullText:
CNET’s key takeaways

The Bluvol I11 Apex cordless hair straightening comb retails for $90.

The I11 Apex is a perfect travel companion for easy touch-ups.

You’ll get up to 45 minutes of styling per charge.

After more than 10 years of wearing my natural curls, I started straightening my hair again. I spent countless hours searching for the best tools and products that would deliver sleek, frizz-free results while protecting my hair from heat damage. The Tymo Ring hair straightening brush stood out to me, and it’s been a good addition to my hair care kit. However, it may have just been replaced by the Bluvol I11 Apex cordless straightening comb.

When the Bluvol I11 Apex arrived, I wasn’t expecting much. I figured it would be good for the occasional touch-up on travel days or even quick fixes if I ever got caught in the rain, but it proved me wrong. It’s lightweight and fits nicely in the hand. From holding it, you can tell it’s well-made. I just couldn’t imagine that something that compact could pack so much heat. 

What the Bluvol I11 Apex looks like straight out of the box.

Putting the Bluvol I11 Apex to the test

To really put the Bluvol I11 Apex to the test, I enlisted my cousin’s help. She’s Gen Z, an expert at all things hair and nails, and most importantly, she has an amazing, thick head of hair. After unboxing the straightening comb, I charged it, and we got started. 

			

More from CNET

It has three heat settings: 320, 365 and 410 degrees Fahrenheit. There’s an LCD screen, which shows the temperature and battery percentage. Switching to a lower or higher setting is simple, using the power button. Once you’ve chosen your temperature, the display will blink as the comb heats up. When it stops blinking, you’re ready to go.

On the first pass, we were impressed with how effortlessly it took my cousin’s hair from curly to straight. The I11 Apex has upgraded ceramic glazed plates throughout the teeth of the comb, which prevent singes and allow multiple passes without damage. Its wide heating area provides even heat distribution for consistent coverage across strands. 

Bluvol says the straightener releases “200 million negative ions to smooth hair and reduce static and frizz.” While I can’t test that accurately, I can attest that it left her hair far smoother than a similar flat iron and required fewer passes to achieve the desired results.

The results on curly hair.

Battery life and charging time

Bluvol includes a charging cable and suggests using a 15-watt or higher adapter when powering up. With the adapter, you’ll go from zero to a full charge in about 2.5 hours. A full charge will give you up to 45 minutes of styling time. We managed to make it about 80% of the way through her hair before needing to recharge.

Who’s the Bluvol I11 Apex for?

This is by far the most impressive cordless straightener I’ve tested, but it might not be for everyone. For folks with shorter hair, this won’t be ideal because the layout of the comb’s teeth doesn’t allow it to really hold super short strands to straighten. The company also notes that if your hair is “very curly,” you might need to use professional styling products for the best results. 

The I11 Apex is the perfect styling companion for when you’re on the go. There are no wires, so you never have to search for an outlet. It’s easy to slip into your handbag, backpack or luggage. There’s even a physical lock switch that prevents it from turning on while it’s stashed away.

Price

This straightening comb typically retails for $90, but Amazon is currently offering a 22% discount for Prime Members.

The specs

Price: $90 retail, but often on sale for less

Battery life: 45 minutes

Wattage: 33 watts

Estimated charge time: 2.5 hours from 0 to 100 with a 15-watt adapter

Number of ports: 1 USB-C port

Max temperature: 410 degrees Fahrenheit (210 degrees Celsius)

Weight: 1.46 pounds

CNET’s buying advice

Whether you want effortless touch-ups on the go or a full straightening solution at home, the Bluvol I11 Apex can get the job done. Want the best of both worlds? Tymo has a new two-in-one straightening brush with a built-in traditional flat iron. If you don’t need the portably of I11 Apex, then it’s worth considering.

She later followed that passion to become a front-end/iOS engineer before switching to writing full-time. Stephanie's writing on technology, health and wellness, movies, television, and much more can be found all over the internet. When she isn't writing, Stephanie can be found reading a good book, baking, obsessing over creating the perfect desk setup, or literally anything that'll help her avoid going outside.

title: An Egg Genius Urged Me to Strain Before Poaching. The Results Were Astounding
snippet: Say goodbye to fluid, flimsy poached eggs when you add this one simple step.
fullText:
Perhaps no other form of egg cookery has so much rhetoric and written words dedicated to it as the elusive poached egg. Poached eggs are humble, but surprisingly complicated to master. Perhaps even more so than the omelet. (In this egg-loving, frequent-egg-cooking author’s opinion.) Even with water as the only other procedural requirement.

If you’ve tried other methods for delivering a perfect poached egg — electric egg cookers, nonstick poaching pans or the seemingly infallible microwave method — and still left unfulfilled or underwhelmed by the outcome, there’s one more pro trick you can try. And here’s a pro tip: Lisa Steele is a fifth-generation chicken keeper and author of Fresh Eggs Daily and In Season: 125+ Sweet and Savory Recipes Celebrating Simple, Fresh Ingredients. She talked me through the single, foolproof step that makes stovetop egg poaching dead simple.

The reason poached eggs are challenging

An egg’s complex structure makes poaching difficult.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Picture it: a pot full of water, maybe with a dash of distilled vinegar, at the gentlest simmer so you don’t subject your delicate egg to a tornado of activity once submerged. You painstakingly crack the egg into a shallow bowl first, and carefully slip it into the pot. Regardless of your good intentions, the egg then clouds the water and turns all wispy, like some sort of blond dementor.

			

More from CNET

You haven’t done anything wrong here; you’ve just failed to understand an egg’s basic structure. “There are actually two components of the egg white, or albumen,” Steele explains. “There’s the thicker part of the white which encases the yolk, and then there’s a separate, thinner layer of egg white around that. It’s the thinner part of the egg white that will spread and turn wispy when you drop an egg into the water.”

The wispy white of an unstrained egg.Pamela Vachon/CNET

To prevent your poached egg from spreading? Strain it

The thing is, you can easily get rid of the thin, watery white part of your egg using one simple tool you’ve probably got in a drawer somewhere and about a minute of your time. Set a small mesh strainer over a cup or bowl, crack the egg into it, and wait.

Pamela Vachon/CNET

“Straining an egg removes the thinner whites that likely won’t adhere to the rest of the egg and result in shaggy, wispy threads,” Steele says. “It won’t affect the flavor outcome of your poached egg, but it is purely for appearance’s sake.” (And potentially your sanity’s or sense of accomplishment’s sake, I might add.)

While the egg’s flavor stays unchanged, for Benedict lovers, straining the egg first slightly improves the white-to-yolk ratio in the poached result and makes the texture more consistent, while also creating a tidy, photogenic package. 

Some patience is required

The thin white will slowly strain itself out.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Once your raw egg is in the strainer, you may notice nothing happens right away, and you may feel the urge to move the egg around a bit to get things going. But don’t zhush, which threatens to scramble the egg. Simply wait for gravity to do its thing; it takes about a minute. It’s akin to what happens when separating whites from yolks, except here you’re separating whites from whites.

	

			

	

			

									

						Fine mesh strainer					

							

		

“Let the thin part of the egg white drip down into the bowl,” Steele says, “then gently slide the egg into the simmering water.” The strainer can also serve as a handy vessel for transferring the egg, especially if you’re only making a single one. If you’re doing multiple eggs and don’t want to risk cooking any remaining white onto the mesh by submerging it, place the strained egg in a small, shallow bowl as usual before easing it into the water. Without the thin, watery white part, you’ll notice a discernible textural difference in the egg even when raw.

Best poaching practices

A gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, is best for poaching.Pamela Vachon/CNET

The straining step alone can almost completely change your poached egg game in an instant, but for the best results, follow the best poaching protocol. You don’t want a full pot of water at a rolling boil like you would for pasta. “Fill a pot or saucepan with a few inches of water and bring to a boil, then turn the heat down to low so the water is just barely simmering with small bubbles floating to the surface,” Steele advises.

A strained egg simmering like a tidy package.Pamela Vachon/CNET

Creating a little whirlpool will further help your remaining egg white stay snug. “Using a wooden spoon or silicone spatula, swirl the water, then gently slide the egg into the center of the whirlpool as you keep swirling for another few seconds around the egg until the egg white turns milky and starts to set up around the yolk,” Steele says. “At this point, you can push the egg to one side, add another egg into the center and repeat the process.”

An unstrained egg on the left versus a strained egg on the right.

A soft-poached egg takes about three minutes, and because you’ve removed the watery part of the egg white, you’ll get a nice firm structure to hold the still-runny yolk — the poached egg ideal.

Since poaching is a delicate process, no matter your new straining habit and how strictly you follow the recommended procedure, “using the freshest eggs possible is very important when you are poaching because the egg white gets even more thin and watery as the egg ages,” Steele says. “The membrane holding the yolk together also weakens, making the yolk more susceptible to breaking.” So if you don’t have them on hand already, get yourself a strainer and some fresh eggs and put this newfound tidbit to the personal test.

Want more cooking hacks?

Cooking bacon in the oven is a great way to make a large batch, but the air fryer method might be even better — and it’s definitely faster. Here are nine more cooking hacks that save time and energy. 

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Pamela Vachon
						

						

							Contributor						
					

											

								

											Pamela is a freelance food and travel writer based in Astoria, Queens. While she writes about most things edible and potable (and accessories dedicated to those topics,) her real areas of expertise are cheese, chocolate, cooking and wine. She's a culinary school grad, certified sommelier, former bartender and fine dining captain with 10 years in the industry. When not sitting at the keys, she leads in-home cheese classes, wine tastings and cocktail demonstrations.

title: Pixel Weather homescreen widget adds manual refresh button
snippet: Following last month’s icon update, Pixel Weather is getting a slightly more substantial update with a refresh button for the homescreen widget. more…
fullText:
Following last month’s icon update, Pixel Weather is getting a slightly more substantial update with a refresh button for the homescreen widget.

This straightforward update adds a refresh button to the top-right corner of the “Forecasted weather” widget. Upon tapping, you’ll briefly see a spinner as the new data loads.

This saves you from having to open the full app if you’re just swiping through your homescreen.

Old vs. new

	

Another tweak we’ve seen in the app is how the Hourly and 10-day forecast cards in the city feed no longer possess left/right buttons to scroll through without swiping. 

Version 1.1.20260716.x of Pixel Weather is now widely rolled out via the Play Store.

In related developments, “Pixel’s exclusive weather app” — along with Recorder — will also be available on all Googlebooks going forward.

title: The clever way Apple embedded Face ID beneath the iPhone 18 Pro screen
snippet: In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display. Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering … more…
fullText:
In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering …

Jony Ive described his long-term vision of the iPhone design as a single slab of glass, and while he is no longer with the company, that goal has remained. Eventually, Apple wants to embed all of the technology requiring screen real estate beneath the display, including both Face ID and front-facing camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro has achieved the first of these, but it was no easy task. Face ID requires infrared light to be both emitted and received by the TrueDepth module – and IR light cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple needed to create gaps between the pixels large enough to allow the IR light to pass between them, but without any visible degradation in the display. To do so, the company’s engineers set out to design a different pixel layout with larger gaps without visibly impacting what can be displayed on those pixels. 

iFixit used a microscope to show this pixel pattern, with Apple confirming to me me that the overall pixel density over the module is reduced by half. This would potentially have created a second problem: half the pixel density might have created a visibly dimmer section of the display, so Apple increases the brightness of these pixels to compensate. There also appears to be an IR pass filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further hiding the components.

The result is remarkable. For all practical purposes, the TrueDepth camera array is impossible to see even when staring at it extremely closely. I couldn’t capture it even using macro photography with different screen colors and lighting conditions. That’s not to say it’s completely impossible to detect, as iFixit’s microscope view shows, but rather that there is absolutely no way you’ll notice it in everyday use.

Right now, that achievement reduces the size of the Dynamic Island, which in turn enables support for three live activities rather than two. In some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden beneath the display. That’s technically possible today, but the compromise in image quality is currently greater than Apple is willing to accept. Solving that issue is a matter of when rather than if.

title: Apple’s dimensional drawings offer a fascinating look at its product designs
snippet: Not everyone knows this (and I won’t even pretend that I did), but Apple publishes remarkably detailed dimensional drawings for dozens of its devices to help accessory makers design products around them. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Not everyone knows this (and I won’t even pretend that I did), but Apple publishes remarkably detailed dimensional drawings for dozens of its devices to help accessory makers design products around them. Here are the details.

Apple hardware, mapped in great detail

For almost 30 years, Jason Kottke has been one of my main sources for interesting content on (and off) the internet that I would most certainly have never discovered otherwise.

A few days ago, he published this post, linking to Apple’s Dimensional Drawings section inside the Accessories area of its developer website.

In a nutshell, this is a repository of incredibly detailed technical drawings of what currently amounts to 96 devices, including the new iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and Series 12, and the AirPods 5.

The list also includes products like the MacBook Neo and the Siri Remote, as well as accessories such as AirTag, AirPods charging cases, and even the Apple Vision Pro’s ZEISS Optical Inserts.

Each document includes precise measurements for everything from the device’s overall dimensions and curves to its buttons, cameras, sensors, speakers, and connectors, along with detailed keepout zones and instructions showing where certain materials should not be placed.

While these documents are meant for accessory makers, they’re also likely to appeal to anyone with even a mild interest in hardware, industrial design, or simply the kind of attention to detail that generally draws people to Apple products in the first place.

title: Google Photos rolling out Redact tool, Mood filters, & more
snippet: Google Photos is rolling out a handful of new features, including a Redact Markup tool and “Moods” on Android. more…
fullText:
Google Photos is rolling out a handful of new features, including a Redact Markup tool and “Moods” on Android.

The upgraded Markup tool adds three features, starting with a Redact pen that lets you blur/pixelate sensitive info in screenshots and images. There are also precise thickness sliders for the Pen and new fonts in the Text tool. This is rolling out globally to Google Photos for Android.

Moods let you easily apply a “nostalgic, vintage-inspired look” to pictures, including Crisp 35mm (film), 2000’s night (digicam), Retro contrast, Night light, Blue Haze, Any Minimalist, and Rich textures. You get slider controls, with each mood “intelligently adapt[ing] to your images.” This is rolling out globally on Android.

There are also 15 new Remix templates, including red carpet moments, whimsical birthday cards, and photo booth shots. This is rolling out in select countries on Android and iOS.

	

Google Photos is also highlighting how the Wardrobe feature is now available in Brazil, India, and the US on Android and iOS. An AI Pro or AI Ultra subscription is required. There’s also the Photos integration in Gemini Spark announced earlier this month.

title: Googlebooks will get full GeForce Now support ‘later this year’
snippet: Nvidia says Google’s new Gemini-infused laptops are slated to get GeForce Now support before the year is up, which is perfect because Googlebooks don’t exactly pack a ton of power. more…
fullText:
Nvidia says Google’s new Gemini-infused laptops are slated to get GeForce Now support before the year is up, which is perfect because Googlebooks don’t exactly pack a ton of power.

The entire Googlebook line was officially announced on September 21, spanning across Acer, Dell, ASUS, HP, and Lenovo. Each has its own draw, but they share the same baseline 16GB of RAM, up to 32GB. Each is equipped with a touchscreen and made from “premium materials,” and they genuinely look great. What qualifies as “premium” ranges from aluminum to carbon fiber. Of course, each has the instantly iconic Glowbar somewhere on the cover, flashing when the laptop is opened or closed.

In essence, Googlebooks run Android, for better or worse. Googlebook OS is almost a parallel operating system, but it and mobile Android go hand-in-hand by design. By nature, that means Google didn’t intend to pack these with discrete graphics cards that could power most games. But that’s why GeForce Now exists, right?

Nvidia announced that GeForce Now would be coming to Googlebooks in an official capacity before the year is up. The original statement only specifies it will arrive “later this year,” which leaves a gap of around three months.

	

That doesn’t mean GeForce Now won’t work with Googlebooks when they become available in October. Google Chrome and even Firefox now support GeForce Now natively through the browser. That means logging into the game streaming website will present a similar experience to a fully dedicated Googlebook app.

Still, an app will likely be a better experience tailored to the hardware outfit Google and its partners pack into the new laptops.

This was expected for a couple of reasons. Google has partnered with Nvidia in the past, and Chromebooks were one of the main targets for GeForce Now in the early days. On top of that, when Googlebooks were first shown off, the majority of titles seen were via GeForce Now and not running on native hardware.

GeForce Now also announced today that a slew of new titles are getting support this week:

title: Apple TV renews French drama ‘Carême’ for season two
snippet: Apple TV today announced that French-language drama “Carême” has been renewed for a second season. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple TV today announced that French-language drama “Carême” has been renewed for a second season. Here are the details.

Apple TV renews ‘Carême’

Earlier today, Apple TV announced that “Carême,” starring Benjamin Voisin, has been renewed for a second season, with filming expected to start next week in Paris.

“Carême” debuted in April last year, and ran for 8 episodes with a 7.9/10 average on IMDb. The drama is based on Ian Kelly’s “Carême: The First Celebrity Chef” book, and is currently nominated for an International Emmy Award in the Drama Series category, as well as two Hollywood Music in Media Awards (HMMA) for its original score and main title.

The 54th International Emmy Awards Gala is set to take place on November 23 in New York City, while the 17th annual HMAA will be held a few days earlier, on November 18, in Hollywood.

Here’s Apple TV on the show’s premise:

“Carême” follows the thrilling story of the world’s first celebrity chef, Antonin Carême (Voisin), who rose from humble beginnings in Paris to the height of culinary stardom in Napoleon’s Europe. While he dreams only of becoming the most famous chef in the world, his talent and ambitions attract the attention of renowned and powerful politicians who use him as a spy for France. Determined to escape poverty and fulfill his dream, Carême can choose revenge or he can have it all — women, wealth, fame — but at what cost? His love? His soul? His life?

The platform didn’t announce a release date for the second season.

iPhone Duo pre-orders start on Friday, October 16, but Apple just announced when you can get an early start on the process. Here are the details.

Starting October 12, and likely running through much of the day October 15, you’ll be able to go to the Apple Store app or Apple’s online store and make your pre-order selections in advance.

title: Honor Magic 9 Pro Max goes official with 8,800 mAh battery, ARRI cameras, Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on. more…
fullText:
Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on.

The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is an all-out flagship with a heavy focus on its cameras, so let’s start there.

Continuing its ARRI partnership that debuted on the Robot Phone, the Magic 9 Pro Max packs a 200MP main camera with “gimbal-level stabilization,” a 200MP telephoto camera with 3.5x optical zoom, and a 50MP ultra-wide camera. Those are arranged on the back in the style of an ARRI cinema camera, and they’re also tuned by ARRI to produce better colors both in photos and videos. Honor is also building out additional hardware including two teleconverter lenses and a “Mobile Video Kit” in partnership with SmallRig.

The front-facing camera is no slouch either, with a 55MP sensor that’s paired with a 3D depth sensing camera for face unlock.

	

The phone surrounding those cameras packs a punch too. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and starts at 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Honor is using its own “Imaging Chip H1” to enhance camera processing, with MagicOS 11 based on Android 17 also available out of the box (with all its Liquid Glass-y-ness). The display is a 6.8-inch 2868×1320 OLED panel with Honor’s NanoCrystal Shield on top (which is both anti-scratch and anti-reflective), 10,000 nits of peak brightness – somehow –, 1-120Hz adaptive refresh rate support, and a 4,320Hz PWM dimming rate for better eye comfort. There’s an 8,800 mAh battery inside with 100W wired charging and 80W wireless, and the whole phone has IP68, IP69, and IP69K dust/water resistance ratings. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max specs

6.8-inch 2868×1320 LTPO OLED display, NanoCrystal glass, 4,320Hz PWM, 10,000 nits peak brightness

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

12/256GB, 12/512GB, 16/512GB, 16/1TB

MagicOS 11 based on Android 17

Rear Cameras: 200MP main (f/1.57), 200MP telephoto (f/2.6, 3.5x optical zoom, up to 200x digital zoom), 50MP ultrawide with autofocus

Front Camera: 55MP + 3D depth-sensing camera

8,800 mAh battery, 100W wired charging, 80W wireless charging

IP68/IP69/IP69K

The Magic 9 Pro Max is available today in China, but Honor says global availability is coming soon. Europe, MEA (Middle East & Africa), SEA (Southeast Asia), and “other key international markets” are all confirmed at this point, but there’s no reason to expect this one in the US. 

Honor also launched the Magic 9 in China.

It has a similar design but with a smaller 6.37-inch display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a very similar camera array, and an 8,000 mAh battery.

title: John Ternus has big plans to make Apple ‘leaner’ and release more products
snippet: New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more. more…
fullText:
New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more.

John Ternus wants to reshape Apple, here’s how

First, the new Apple CEO wants to release more products faster than before, including becoming “more experimental.” One idea is to shake up Apple’s release calendar and rely less on the typical spring-and-fall cadence, instead releasing more new products throughout the year. 

Ternus also wants to “create a leaner organization with a greater focus on engineering.” This includes several cost-cutting measures and restructuring. For instance, one change is “eliminating some middle-management positions to reduce the layers separating engineers from senior executives.”

The report says Apple has dismissed “a number of engineering program managers, or EPMs,” in its hardware engineering division over the last two weeks. Bloomberg describes these roles as having been “central to Apple’s product-development process for decades,” responsible for “managing timelines and coordinating work across teams.”

“The cuts affected several program managers, including roughly half a dozen directors, one of the company’s most senior employee levels,” the report says. “Those employees were given just weeks to find other positions within Apple. Those who don’t secure new roles will be laid off later this year.”

Bloomberg says the cost-cutting measures could go much broader than that, though. Ternus has reportedly advocated for Apple to be “leaner” for years:

Ternus, 51, has advocated for a leaner organization for years. While leading hardware engineering, he told employees during an all-hands meeting that Apple should hire fewer people, ask more of its existing engineers and reduce organizational bloat. During a presentation, he showed a slide charting annual headcount growth and argued that the company should be accomplishing more with fewer employees.

Furthermore, Apple reportedly scrapped a plan over the summer to lay off 5,000 AppleCare employees, believing that AI-powered agents could handle those responsibilities.

At the same time, Ternus wants Apple to increase revenue from Apple’s services division alongside Eddy Cue and CFO Kevan Parekh. “They have discussed launching new services and extracting more revenue from existing products and offerings,” the report says.

Ultimately, one source told Bloomberg that things are “hectic” inside Apple right now:

“Everything is a lot more hands-on than it used to be,” said one person familiar with the situation. “It’s hectic right now.” That person and others said managers in product-development groups are being pushed to deliver more products, more frequently and on shorter timelines.

You can read the full report at Bloomberg. It’s a fascinating piece that I highly recommend reading in full.

title: Pet Hair Everywhere? This $30 Roller Removes It From Places a Vacuum Simply Can’t
snippet: The SandBar helps in the battle against pet hair and rogue bits of kitty litter.
fullText:
Among the many joys of having a cat is the daily battle with the mess they leave behind. No matter what you try, finding litter and pet hair on furniture or in your bed is inevitable — either they track it in, or you do. If you’re a pet parent like me, this means searching for additional bits of litter and stray hairs that find their way into places you really don’t want them, including the bed. Short of pulling the sheets off entirely, few fixes exist.

I took a chance and tested the SandBar Roller, a $30 dual-roll lint roller, to see if it can make it easier to keep stray hair and litter at bay. I also put it through the paces for other lint-roller tasks like dusting and cleaning floors. Here’s how it fared.

How SandBar Roller differs from other lint rollers

The SandBar Roller Starter Kit I tested included the roller head, an extendable handle and two preinstalled lint rolls.John Carlsen/CNET

The SandBar Roller’s appeal lies in its two large lint rollers instead of one. While the idea doesn’t seem like much of a departure from a typical large lint roller, I couldn’t find any other dual-roller designs intended for use between bedsheets like SandBar. By arranging the rollers in this way, SandBar can clean the top and bottom sheets simultaneously without getting stuck.

			

More from CNET

	

			

	

			

									

						The Best Handheld Vacuums, Tested by CNET					

							

		

While SandBar markets its proprietary lint rolls as stronger than normal rolls, they’re not much different from what you’ll find on the extra-large pet hair version of the Scotch-Brite lint roller. Both are 8 inches wide, with an inner diameter of 1.5 inches. Much to SandBar’s credit, its six-pack of refill rolls is just $20, which is very competitive with other lint roll refills I found on Amazon, with the optional subscription price dropping to just $16 for each one-, two- or three-month delivery.

Testing the SandBar Roller

The extendable handle is very practical.John Carlsen/CNET

Ostensibly, this design targets coastal homes, where sand gets everywhere — hence the SandBar name. While I don’t live on the coast, I’ve experienced sand in my bed while traveling, or after day trips to the desert, and cat litter is a near-daily occurrence. With that in mind, I conducted a series of informal tests to see how the SandBar Roller holds up.

Upon putting SandBar between the sheets, I noticed it moved fairly smoothly, at least until it snagged on some sheets that were too loose. It didn’t jam, but that means it works better for beds with the sheet firmly tucked at the foot — something I don’t do for various sleep-friendly reasons. Still, it worked well after tightening the sheets a bit, even snagging a few cat hairs and litter fragments. It’s a nice alternative to washing the sheets as frequently as I have to now.

I like the stickiness of the rolls, which is satisfyingly tacky without leaving residue or making it difficult to pull off used strips.John Carlsen/CNET

The SandBar removed cat fur from hard-to-reach places

Next, I wanted to see how it handled cleaning smart window shades and curtains, which often collect fur as my cat patrols windows a few times a day. It was a little more awkward, but taking the handle off proved effective, and the sticky roller collected a substantial amount of fur. I had to peel off multiple sheets because of the amount of fur, but it took only a few passes to clean the curtain. The SandBar Roller was very useful on furniture and pet beds, but I noticed that being too aggressive can occasionally dislodge a roll.

The SandBar Roller left a fairly clean surface when I dusted off a TV cabinet and soundbar. Still, I wouldn’t trade it out for the duster and handheld vacuum I usually use. Likewise, it did well on the linoleum floor and carpet near my cat’s litter box, but still I prefer the cleaner result I get from vacuuming.

Should you buy the SandBar Roller?

The specialized design does its job well, but is probably too niche for people who aren’t pet parents or near vast swathes of sand.John Carlsen/CNET

At $30, the SandBar Roller is unlikely to break anyone’s budget, especially when you can find similarly large bed lint rollers for the same price. In that context alone, including the cost of refill rolls, it’s probably as good as any other option. Still, the dual-roll design’s ability to get between sheets is a compelling reason to consider the SandBar Roller over the competition. The design suits households that typically deal with a lot of sand and litter in the beds. I could even see myself taking it camping for quick dirt cleanup in a sleeping bag.

However, I wouldn’t recommend it for short-term beach house rentals because it cuts corners — new guests expect clean sheets when they arrive. That said, making a SandBar Roller available during a guest’s visit could be worthwhile to improve their experience, as long as you leave instructions explaining what it’s for and how it works.

If you don’t need the second roll — and mainly deal with pet hair on furniture — the ChomChom Roller doesn’t need refill rolls, making it a much better option for $25. Likewise, a handheld vacuum can do the same job with a bit more flexibility around the house — though it’s not quiet enough to use when others are sleeping. While it’s nice to have so many options, it’s always worth going with what works best for your needs and situation.

title: iOS 27 brings three key new features to Find My
snippet: iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new.

iOS 27: What’s new for Find My?

Apple touts three changes to Find My in iOS 27:

More flexible sharing options

UI enhancements

Apple Watch updates

First, more flexible sharing options in Find My give you more control over when and for how long you share your location with others. “Share your location for a custom duration or until a set date and time,” Apple says. You can also now “pause sharing with people individually, whenever you want.”

One of the bigger changes here is that you can now hide your location from a specific person without sending them any notification or alert. The other person won’t be notified when you pause, stop, or resume sharing your location with them.

Previously, you could turn off your location in the Find My app altogether, which wouldn’t send a notification. This, however, hid your location from everyone. In iOS 27, you can disable your location for specific people. 

To manage this, you’ll see a new “Hide Location” toggle on each person’s card in the Find My app. If you pause sharing your location with someone, they will see a “No Location Found” message in their Find My app.

Design changes

As for the UI enhancements, Find My in iOS 27 has been refreshed with a new Liquid Glass interface. The app largely missed out on Liquid Glass in iOS 26, but this year it has a new tab bar design that matches Apple’s other apps.

The Find My interface now also shows more specific location information on the app’s main page. This means you don’t have to tap on each person to view exactly what street they’re on at any given moment.

There is also new iconography in the Find My app in iOS 27. The “Items” tab, for example, is now denoted by a new AirTag-style icon.

Apple Watch updates

Finally, for cellular Apple Watch users, sharing your location will automatically use your Apple Watch when you’re away from your iPhone or iPad. 

Also on Apple Watch, there’s a redesigned, unified Find My app that integrates people, items, and devices into one interface.

title: iPhone video stabilization continues to wow me in the iPhone 18 Pro
snippet: I first talked about how much iPhone video stabilization impressed me when I tested it on the iPhone 13 Pro back in 2021. It’s been improved significantly since then, with both the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro having a version Apple refers to as “ultra-stabilized video.” While it doesn’t sound as sexy as some features, it makes a massive difference to the usability of the iPhone for handheld shooting – and my latest test really drove home just how good it is today … more…
fullText:
I first talked about how much iPhone video stabilization impressed me when I tested it on the iPhone 13 Pro back in 2021. It’s been improved significantly since then, with both the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro having a version Apple refers to as “ultra-stabilized video.”

While it doesn’t sound as sexy as some features, it makes a massive difference to the usability of the iPhone for handheld shooting – and my latest test really drove home just how good it is today … 

I have a mini tripod and GorillaPod that I carry with me when I know I’m going to want to shoot some iPhone video footage, but of course, one of the huge benefits of an iPhone is that it’s the camera you always have with you. There are times when I spot an opportunity for a shot and don’t have a tripod with me. 

It’s often possible to improvise, whether that’s by leaning the iPhone against a railing or bracing myself against something like a lamppost. But there are times when I rely on the built-in video stabilization on iPhones, and in the most recent example, shooting with the iPhone 18 Pro, I was incredibly impressed. 

A riverboat trip down the Thames demonstrated that there are times when the iPhone’s built-in video stabilization feature is actually better than a tripod. That’s because the boat rocks around a fair bit, which would have meant a stable shot of the boat with the scenery outside moving around. The iPhone reliably stabilized to the outside world with the boat moving around in the foreground.

That ability to keep the horizon true no matter what movements the platform makes is something we don’t even get with a typical gimbal. Most consumer-grade ones smooth out movement rather than eliminating it. It’s only with high-end professional gimbals and the type of giro mount designed for marine and helicopter use that we get truly locked horizons.

The iPhone 18 Pro’s ultra-stabilization feature honestly delivers this level of performance, and that’s a pretty incredible feature to have as standard in the stock Camera app with no external hardware required.

Check out the sample footage below. If you don’t want to take the full ride, the Tower Bridge section starting here is probably the best showcase for the feature. But if you do want to enjoy the London tourist experience, hit C to switch on the captions for all the bridge names and a few other comments, including pointing out Apple’s UK campus.

fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m going crazy over the NYT’s list of the best TV shows of the 21st century, redoing all of my vibe-projects with Opus 5.5, girding my loins for another Witcher 3 play-through now that the free remaster is out, and devouring Colson Whitehead’s new novel, Cool Machine.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

October 4th marks 10 years since Google debuted the Pixel, and over the next few days we plan to dive into the brand’s storied legacy. What started with a couple of HTC-built devices has expanded into an ecosystem that includes budget and flagship smartphones, smartwatches, earbuds, tablets, and more. 

	

The Pixel has served several purposes for Google throughout its lifespan, beginning as an extension of Nexus’s “Android best practices” before morphing into something a bit more complicated and abstract. When it debuted, Google emphasized the Pixel’s camera advantages, of which there were many, along with timely annual platform updates that arrived months before other Android devices.

As time went on, the Pixel brand came to encompass more than just smartphones; the company debuted its Tensor SoC inside the Pixel 6, and expanded the line to include the Pixel Watch, Pixel Buds, and a couple of failed Pixel-branded tablets. 

Perhaps the most remarkable thing about the Pixel lineup is its longevity; under Rick Osterloh, the brand has become synonymous with deep integration into Google’s services — of late, particularly Gemini — and a steward of thoughtful software and hardware design. The company’s products have made inroads in many markets, but still represent a single-digit share in most, including the US (despite solid year-over-year growth in 2026).

It’s perhaps also worth pointing out that the Pixel lineup has persevered in spite of many challenges, from major hardware issues with the Pixel 2 and 3 series to Covid-related supply constraints in the Pixel 5 to reputation-harming modem performance in the Pixel 6. It really wasn’t until 2023’s Pixel 8 series that Google shook its image as a mediocre hardware vendor and married superlative hardware with delightful software.

Today, the Pixel lineup is both the best and most predictable it’s ever been. The Pixel 11 series is yet another iteration on a design that debuted in 2021 with the Pixel 6. The Pixel Watch has looked identical since its 2022 debut. The Pixel Buds are fine but not competitive. The Pixel Tablet appears to be dead, and there’s no sign of a Pixelbook successor on the horizon.

Ten years in, is the Pixel brand where Google wanted it to be, with its cultural influence outpacing its financial viability? Perhaps not, but it’s also not likely to disappear anytime soon, which speaks volumes about its importance, both to the company and the community that keeps it in the conversation.

🤝 Cc: Max Weinbach

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Max Weinbach, who used to contribute to 9to5Google and is now a tech analyst with Creative Strategies.

Who are you?

I’m Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies. You might also know me from writing about phones at XDA and 9to5Google, or from spending way too much time talking about technology on Twitter.

What do you do for work?

I research and write about consumer technology, especially phones, PCs, chips, and AI. A lot of my work now is figuring out what AI can actually do when you give it a real task, real data, and the tools to finish the job. I also consider my job to be just knowing a lot about many different technology topics. 

That has turned into building things, too. We’ve been working on Diligence Stack and practical agent benchmarks, testing how the model, the tools, and the surrounding software affect the result. I want to know whether something can produce useful work and how much fixing it needs afterward. That tells me a lot more than a score by itself.

What do you do for fun?

I build things and play games. There’s quite a bit of overlap between my hobbies and my work. I’ll get interested in some software problem and end up with another side project. I’ve been spending a lot of time on native apps and experimenting with AI agents.

Reviewing gaming hardware is also a very convenient excuse to play something I’ve been putting off. That’s how I finally got around to Alan Wake 2 and picked Spider-Man 2 back up. 

On top of that, the classics of harassing playing with my dog and going to the gym. I’ve spent a lot of time learning about health and wellness. It’s just interesting to learn about and put into practice for me!

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I’m still excited about it, but I care a lot about the experience of actually using something. A great spec sheet only gets you so far if the laptop is annoying, the software gets in your way, or the AI needs more supervision than the task was worth.

Some of my favorite products are the ones that are almost boring because they get the basics right. A comfortable laptop that runs the things I need, lasts a long time, and doesn’t have some weird deal-breaking issue is genuinely exciting to me. I’m also interested in how much easier it’s becoming to build the software I want to use.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

ChatGPT. I love ChatGPT as a product. It’s one of those apps that just let me kinda delegate whatever I want, and it will simply do it. It’s good for research, good for building one-off apps here and there, and just a great platform to help with anything I can think of. It doesn’t replace any actual work for me, but makes that work much easier and quicker. 

Whoop. Technically, an app and a product, but the product powers the app so I’m going with it. It’s one of my favorite ways to track health and wellness because it’s the first that has basically nailed the feeling of recovery and strain on a daily basis. In the morning I actually try to guess what the number will be based on what I feel, and I get it pretty close every morning. 

X/Twitter. X is one of my favorite ways to actually consume media and news, share my thoughts, keep up with friends. Yes, I know this is such a normal choice and nothing unique here, but I don’t know, I really like the app. My life would be very different without it.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Plaud’s Note Pro MagSafe thing. It’s fantastic, and makes my life significantly easier all around when it comes to notes. I tend to have a good memory when it comes to meetings, so I tend to not take notes. That only gets you so far when it comes to specific details, and I find actually writing notes distracting. This thing solves it for me: take a recording, transcribe, and generate key notes while I can listen. Yes, voice memos exist on every phone and watch but I like this a lot more.

How does AI fit into your life right now?

It’s a big part of how I build and research things. I use agents for coding, testing ideas, and working through problems, then look at what they actually produce. The useful question for me is how close they get to a result I can use.

One recent example is having agents write and optimize Metal kernels for a local model, testing changes on the hardware as they go. I still choose between cloud and local models based on the job. Having the option to use both is valuable. 

I also have a ton of little ideas of how things should work, apps I want, little fun animations or widgets or whatever I can think of for my different products or phones or connecting to Siri and I can just make it by dictating into a magic box and an hour later it’s installed on my products.

What is a recent TV show you loved?

Lanterns, I think it’s just a fun good show that, while it’s not done yet, is just fun. It’s a superhero show that’s not a superhero show entirely. It’s simply a great story told extremely well with characters I like.

What is a recent game you loved?

Marvel’s Spider-Man 2. I bought a PS5 to play it and then never finished it, so reviewing the MSI Claw gave me a good excuse to start again. It looks fantastic, and the movement and combat work really well on a controller. I ended up getting into the game rather than constantly thinking about the hardware. When the testing was done, I kept playing.

What is something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Spending time with Malibu, my Goldendoodle. It’s a good reason to put the computer down for a bit. Otherwise, I enjoy being online. It’s a good way to connect with the world and what interests me. I know a lot of people want to disconnect because the world is stressful, but that’s reality and I like it. I’d rather absorb it all and just make using technology, or being online, a normal thing rather than seeing it as this overarching bad thing that is ruining lives.

title: Duo-Man turns your 2026 iPhone Duo into a 1980s Sony Walkman
snippet: Long before the iPod, the Sony Walkman was the device of choice for those who wanted to add a soundtrack to their life. Now a Duo-Man app recreates the experience for those of us old enough to have owned one, and you’ll be able to use it with Apple Music … more…
fullText:
Long before the iPod, the Sony Walkman was the device of choice for those who wanted to add a soundtrack to their life. Now a Duo-Man app recreates the experience for those of us old enough to have owned one, and you’ll be able to use it with Apple Music …

Prior to the Walkman, if you wanted to listen to music on the move, your options were limited. Most cassette players of the time were heavy and bulky. When Sony took an audio recorder designed for journalists and shrunk it into the smallest possible cassette player, it quickly became an iconic product.

Developer Vidit Bhargava created the app at a hackathon – and given that many of those present would never have seen one, he brought along the real thing to show them what it looked like.

Duo-Man offers the complete walkman experience on the iPhone Duo. Open the Duo to pick and 'insert' the cassette, Close the Duo to start listening.

Yes, I actually recorded the button clicks and static noise from a real Walkman!

It was fun making this at @bitrig hacks today. pic.twitter.com/juSrLhofrH

— Vidit Bhargava (@viditb) September 27, 2026

You open the Duo, choose your album to insert the tape, and then close it to play.

Bhargava said he originally only created it as a demo app for fun, but will now be releasing it as an actual app. The best comment in the X thread is this one, an image that will only make sense to people of a certain age.

title: iPhone Duo video shows left-handed use for new model
snippet: iPhone Duo is less than a month away, but many prospective buyers are still wondering how well the device will work in left-handed use. Here’s a video that shows a left-handed example. more…
fullText:
iPhone Duo is less than a month away, but many prospective buyers are still wondering how well the device will work in left-handed use. Here’s a video that shows a left-handed example.

Here’s how iPhone Duo works in left-handed use

If you’re left-handed, the iPhone Duo may be exciting but also spark some questions. That’s because the new foldable is clearly designed for right-handed use primarily.

When using the outer display, iPhone Duo’s left side is one straight flat edge because it’s where the hinge is. But the right side has curved corners, inviting you to open it like a book.

The dock is also located on the right side of the display, and Apple hasn’t said if an accessibility setting will let you move it to the left.

So how will left-handed users fare with the iPhone Duo? 

Since everyone’s hand size is different, testing the device in an Apple Store will be the only way to know for sure. But I recently came across a video of iPhone Duo being used left-handed, and it’s the first time I’ve seen someone try it.

Here’s the video from Tom Hitchins (@bytereview) on Instagram:

Hitchins looks a little uncomfortable with the device, but as he explains in the comments, that’s because he’s actually right-handed. Thus, his left-handed test was for others’ sake.

	

The video says “works well enough” as Hitchins is able to reach from the left side all the way to the dock on the right. But you’ll want to test yourself to be sure.

I’m right-handed, but use my iPhone in my left hand so that my dominant hand is kept free. I suspect there are plenty of other right-handed users who do the same. So I’m a little unsure about the adjustment to using iPhone Duo in my right hand, but will report back once I’m able to test it.

title: Apple Wallet in iOS 27 adds feature that’s been on my wishlist for years
snippet: iOS 27 adds a variety of new features and changes for Apple Wallet, including one that’s been on my wishlist for years: the ability to import physical passes. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds a variety of new features and changes for Apple Wallet, including one that’s been on my wishlist for years: the ability to import physical passes.

iOS 27 lets you import physical passes, membership cards, event tickets into Apple Wallet

Apple Wallet offers a host of features to help you replace your physical wallet and keys.

It holds credit cards, driver’s licenses, transit cards, boarding passes, event tickets, car keys, home keys, hotel keys, and more.

And with iOS 27, the Wallet app takes another big step toward being the only wallet you need.

That’s because you can now import physical passes, tickets, membership cards, and the like into Apple Wallet.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:

iPhone and Apple Watch users will be able to create and store passes in Apple Wallet from physical cards, like loyalty or membership cards, eliminating the need to fumble through pockets and bags. With Siri mode in the Camera app, users simply point their iPhone at any physical card with a barcode or even screenshot a digital one, and they’ll be prompted to save it to Apple Wallet. Users can also create and add a pass directly from Apple Wallet. Once added, passes are ready to present as a barcode or QR code right from their iPhone or Apple Watch.

Digital passes are a lot more common today than when Apple Wallet first launched. But they aren’t available for everything.

I definitely still encounter businesses and events that utilize physical passes exclusively. And when I do, it adds a little anxiety to my life because I then need to remember to bring those passes with me at the right time.

But with iOS 27, everything can start going in the Wallet app, which is always with me. By putting everything in Wallet, the mental burden of remembering to bring something extra is suddenly gone.

title: Google Messages finally rolls out new long-press menu with precise copying
snippet: After testing got underway in January, Google Messages is finally widely rolling out a new long-press menu in conversations. more…
fullText:
After testing got underway in January, Google Messages is finally widely rolling out a new long-press menu in conversations.

This new design replaces the top toolbar that housed various actions. Google only surfaced three actions with everything else in an overflow menu.

	

Upon long-pressing on a chat message or image, Google will show a floating menu with Remix (photos), Reply, Forward, Copy (text), Star, Delete, Select more, Info, and Save (photos).

Each action is accompanied by an icon at the front for quick scanning, while Copy lets you highlight a specific part of the message by pressing down and dragging the bubble. Previously, you could only copy the entire message.

	

If you’ve selected the newest message in a thread, Google will somewhat center it with a bouncy animation and haptic feedback. Messages prominently blurs the background layer when this menu is active. The row of emoji and “Create” Photomoji shortcuts is unchanged.

As of today, we’re seeing the new Google Messages long-press menu widely rolled out with stable version 20260910_03_RC02. There is a server-side component, so be sure to Force stop from the App info menu if it’s not yet live.

title: Motorola’s wide Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor might be very tiny and called ‘Razr Flex’
snippet: According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs. more…
fullText:
According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs.

Specs for Motorola’s wide foldable were shared by Android Headlines alongside a possible name for the device – “Razr Flex.” That’s apparently the name being used internally around the device, so it’s unclear if that would be used as a consumer-facing name. The codename is “Parker,” the report claims.

Much more interesting are the details around the side of this foldable, which shares the same general form factor as Samsung’s smash hit Galaxy Z Fold 8, just in a much smaller footprint. Apparently, the outer display is just 4.97-inches in size – the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is 5.5-inches – while the inner display is less than 7-inches across. Very tiny by modern phone standards, even in this new form factor.

The leaked specs include:

	

4.97-inch outer display (1736×1140)

6.92-inch inner display (2364×1728)

110x149x5.8mm unfolded | 110x76x12.6mm folded

215g

Snapdragon 8 Gen 5

12GB RAM

256GB of storage

5,000 mAh battery with Qi2 (magnets unclear)

IP48/49

50MP main/50MP ultrawide rear cameras, 32MP selfie cameras

PANTONE Coriander, PANTONE Dark Botanical Garden

It’s important to stress just how much smaller this is compared to other wide foldables. iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than Samsung’s phone, but has roughly the same screen sizes. The closest comparison is the Xiaomi 18 Fold, which has a 5.38-inch outer display, but even that still has a 7.58-inch inner panel. 

The specs are otherwise pretty familiar to the full-size Razr Fold that launched earlier this year.

Concept renders were also shared, but they’re explicitly not based on, well, anything except sketches and Motorola’s general design language – take them not just with a grain of salt, but maybe a whole container.

The “Razr Flex” is said to be launching this year with a “mid-December” debut mentioned.

There’s also Pixel Watch sleep sync that pauses music, disables touch controls, and silences notifications on the Pixel Buds. Finally, you will be able to trigger Live translate by tapping your Pixel Buds.

title: Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On leak, showing what they look like when worn
snippet: Once rumored to go by a different name, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds On open-ear designs have appeared with a little more detail in new images, suggesting these earbuds might become official sooner rather than later. more…
fullText:
Once rumored to go by a different name, Samsung’s Galaxy Buds On open-ear designs have appeared with a little more detail in new images, suggesting these earbuds might become official sooner rather than later.

The Galaxy Buds On have been leaked several times over the last couple of months, though rumors suggested the earbuds would go by “Galaxy Buds Able” instead of the “Galaxy Buds On” name. That information was gleaned from Samsung’s Wearable app in early July, though the first of the two names seems to be an internal moniker.

New images of the Galaxy Buds On have surfaced (via Android Headlines). Previously, we’ve seen detailed renders and icon images, but nothing that looks like it could be official from Samsung. The new photos look a little cleaner, and one looks likely to be from the marketing team.

The Galaxy Buds On images also show what they look like when worn properly – that is, clipped around the ears rather than resting in them. It’s also a different style from the open-ear design worn over the ear. They look uncomfortable, but the design is already plentiful in certain regions, suggesting it’s a popular form factor.

	

It’s hard to pick up any details from the earbud images or to determine which port is the driver and which is the microphone for ambient noise detection. Even if that were determined properly, there’s no telling how they’ll sound prior to release.

The Galaxy Buds On were reported to have a few interesting features when previous images were leaked, such as an “Auto Volume” setting and head-nod and shake gesture control. Samsung Galaxy users will also have voice memos automatically transcribed to text.

Other devices like the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra have been circulating alongside the Galaxy Buds On, suggesting Samsung is gearing up for another launch soon. When that is, there’s no telling right now.

Select Phone only.
